items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Most cities that launched door-to-door vaccination drives in the 2010s saw only modest gains in childhood immunization rates. Riverton, a mid-sized port city, was a striking exception to that pattern. ______ its rate climbed from 71 percent to 94 percent in just two years, a jump larger than that recorded by any other participating city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says Riverton was an exception to the pattern of modest gains. The sentence after it backs up that same claim with vivid evidence: a 23-point jump, bigger than any other city's. Because sentence two confirms and strengthens sentence one, 'Indeed' is the right transition.

A.why: You saw a contrast between Riverton's big jump and the modest gains elsewhere, and you let that surface contrast drive your choice. But the sentence right before the blank already says Riverton was an exception. The jump confirms that claim instead of turning against it.

C.why: You treated the rise in the rate as one example drawn from a larger group. The rise isn't a sample of several exceptions. It is the evidence for the one exception already named, so it confirms the point rather than illustrating it.

D.why: You read a cause-and-effect link that isn't there. Being an exception didn't cause Riverton's rate to climb. The climb is the reason Riverton counts as an exception.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Astronomers value the planned Halvorsen Array for two separate capabilities. First, its twelve dishes can be linked electronically to act as a single telescope with extraordinary resolution. ______ the array can observe in several radio frequencies at once, allowing researchers to follow fast-changing sources such as pulsars without switching instruments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says there are two capabilities, and the second sentence gives the first one. The sentence after the blank gives the second: a new item of the same kind. An addition word is needed, so 'In addition' is correct.

B.why: You assumed the first capability produces the second. Linking dishes for resolution doesn't cause the array to observe in several frequencies at once. The two are independent features.

C.why: You read the second capability as replacing the first. The passage says astronomers value both, so nothing is being swapped out.

D.why: You mixed up reinforcing a point with adding one. 'In other words' would mean sentence two restates the resolution feature, but it describes a completely different capability, the second of the two.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Nutritionist Ama Owusu argues that the fiber in whole lentils sharply slows the rate at which sugars from a meal enter the bloodstream. Her 2021 feeding trial offers strong support for that view. ______ participants who ate a lentil side dish with white rice showed blood-glucose peaks nearly 30 percent lower than those of participants who ate the rice alone, and the effect lasted well into the afternoon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says the trial strongly supports Owusu's view. The sentence after it gives the striking result that shows how strong that support is. Because sentence two confirms and intensifies sentence one, 'Indeed' is the most logical choice.

A.why: You took the comparison between the two groups of participants as a contrast between the sentences. The lower peaks agree with the claim that the trial supports Owusu, so a word that pushes back doesn't fit.

B.why: 'Similarly' needs a second, parallel case that resembles the first. The glucose result isn't a separate case like the trial. It is the trial's own finding, so it reinforces the point rather than comparing it to something else.

D.why: You read the result as replacing something in the sentence before. Nothing is rejected or swapped out. The result supports exactly what came before.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Cover crops such as rye and clover, planted between growing seasons, benefit farms in several distinct ways. Their dense roots hold soil in place during winter storms, greatly reducing erosion. ______ when the plants are cut down in spring, they decompose into organic matter that helps the soil retain water through the dry summer months.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says cover crops help in several ways. The second gives one benefit, erosion control, and the sentence after the blank gives another, water retention. A second, parallel item calls for an addition word, so 'Moreover' is correct.

A.why: You read the water-retention benefit as an example of the sentence right before the blank. It isn't a case of erosion control. It is a separate benefit, another member of the 'several ways'.

B.why: You sensed a shift, from winter to spring and from roots to decomposition, and read it as a contrast. Both sentences describe benefits pointing the same direction, so nothing is being conceded or reversed.

C.why: You assumed the erosion control causes the water retention. The decaying plant matter helps the soil hold water whether or not the roots prevented erosion. The two benefits are parallel, not cause and effect.

items.stimulus: Folklorists who study the Appalachian 'Jack tales' note that the stories served more than one purpose for the families who told them. They entertained children during long winter evenings, when farm work slowed and households gathered by the fire. ______ the tales handed down practical lessons, since Jack's success usually depended on patience, thrift, and a sharp eye for a stranger's intentions.

items.explanation: The first sentence says the tales served more than one purpose. The second names entertainment, and the sentence after the blank names a different purpose, teaching practical lessons. A new item of the same kind calls for 'Additionally'.

D.why: You assumed the lessons follow from the entertainment. The passage doesn't say the tales taught lessons because they were entertaining. It lists the two purposes side by side.

C.why: 'Likewise' needs a second creature or behavior that resembles the first. The second sentence describes the same wrasses and the same boldness, so it reinforces the point rather than drawing a comparison.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Seismologist Rena Okafor has spent a decade monitoring the Tarsin Fault, which typically releases strain through thousands of tremors too faint for nearby residents to feel. The magnitude 6.1 earthquake that struck the fault in 2019 was therefore a striking departure from its usual behavior. ______ in the forty years of records preceding that event, no tremor on the fault had exceeded magnitude 3.5.

items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says the 2019 quake was a striking departure from the fault's usual behavior. The sentence after it backs up that claim: for forty years nothing larger than magnitude 3.5 had happened, which is exactly why a 6.1 counts as an outlier. The second sentence strengthens the first rather than adding a separate point, so you need an emphasis word. 'Indeed' is that word.

C.why: You treated the second sentence as a result of the first. The forty quiet years came before the 2019 quake, so they can't be its consequence. They are evidence for calling it a departure.

D.why: 'Instead' means one thing is taking the place of another. Nothing is being replaced here. The second sentence confirms the first.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Before a revised coastal chart is released, cartographers at the national hydrographic office check it against three independent sources. They start by comparing every depth figure on the draft with the most recent sonar surveys of the seabed. ______ they cross-reference each lighthouse, buoy, and beacon against the coast guard's current registry of navigational aids. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage describes three separate checks, and the words 'start by' and 'Lastly' mark the first and third. The sentence after the blank gives the second check, which is a new item of the same kind as the first. That is simple addition, so 'In addition' is correct.

A.why: You noticed the umbrella phrase 'three independent sources' and expected an example. But the sentence just before the blank is already one specific check. The registry check isn't an instance of the sonar comparison. It is a separate check that comes next.

B.why: 'Even so' introduces something that goes against what came before. The registry check doesn't undercut the sonar comparison. It is simply the next step in the same procedure.

D.why: You read the second check as a result of the first. Checking depth figures doesn't lead to checking lighthouses and buoys. The two are independent steps in a planned sequence.

items.stimulus: To slow drivers on Harlow Avenue, traffic engineer Lucía Brandt recommended that the city narrow the street from four lanes to two and widen its sidewalks. B.why: 'Otherwise' introduces what would happen if something else were not true. The plaza vote isn't a hypothetical alternative. It is what the council actually did.

C.why: 'For instance' introduces one example drawn from a larger group. The passage doesn't set up a group of actions to sample from. The plaza vote is the single action that shows how far the council went.

items.stimulus: Astronomers have generally expected comets to lose most of their surface ice after a few hundred passes near the Sun, fading into dim, inactive bodies. C.why: You compared the bright coma with the 'dim, inactive bodies' mentioned earlier. The sentence before the blank already says Halvorsen-4 is the exception. The coma supports that point rather than contrasting with it.

items.stimulus:

| 3 | 2,160 |

items.stem: Which of the following functions models this relationship, where $u(t)$ is the number of registered users $t$ years after 2020?
items.explanation: Each value is 1.2 times the one before it, since $2{,}160 \div 1{,}800 = 1.2$ and $2{,}592 \div 2{,}160 = 1.2$. C.why: You worked back only one year, from $t = 2$ to $t = 1$. You need one more step to reach $t = 0$.

D.why: You drew a straight line through the first two rows. It predicts 2,520 users at $t = 4$ instead of 2,592, because the users grow by a constant percentage, not a constant number.

items.stimulus: Archaeologists studying a sealed storage jar estimate that its residue first contained $96$ micrograms of an organic marker compound. The amount of the compound halves every $1{,}400$ years.
items.stem: How many years after the sample is sealed will exactly $6$ micrograms of the compound remain?

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: In the tuning system used for a study of piano repertoire, the reference pitch has a frequency of $220$ hertz. Each time a note is $12$ semitones higher, its frequency doubles.
items.stem: What is the frequency, in hertz, of a note that is $36$ semitones above the reference pitch?
items.explanation: The model is $f(n) = 220(2)^{n/12}$, where $n$ is the number of semitones above the reference pitch. For $n = 36$ the exponent is $\frac{36}{12} = 3$, so $f(36) = 220(2)^3 = 220 \times 8 = 1{,}760$ hertz.

D.why: You doubled four times instead of three. 36 semitones is $\frac{36}{12} = 3$ doublings.

items.stimulus: Drypoint plates in printmaking wear down as prints are pulled from them. A printmaking studio gives a new plate a quality score of 100. Its model says that each print reduces the score by 10% of the score just before that print.

items.stimulus: Some astronomers have argued that the reddish surfaces of certain small icy bodies indicate that the bodies formed beyond Neptune. results from exposure to radiation rather than from methanol-rich ice
is more common among bodies from near Saturn than among bodies from beyond Neptune
does not by itself establish that a body formed beyond Neptune rather than near Saturn
items.explanation: The chain runs like this: reddening comes from methanol-rich ice, and that ice could form in two regions, beyond Neptune and near Saturn. meets a requirement for forming the memory cells tied to lasting protection
keeps antigen in the lymph nodes longer than any other formulation does
works chiefly by strengthening the vaccine's initial antibody response

identify which individual residents have become infected
detect rising influenza infections before clinic counts show them
confirm influenza outbreaks only after clinics have reported them

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Seismologist Ines Varga studies slow slip events, episodes in which a fault moves gradually over weeks without producing strong shaking. Her models indicate that such events can shift stress onto neighboring locked sections of a fault, and earlier research has shown that added stress on a locked section increases the chance that it will rupture in a large earthquake. In 2023, GPS stations recorded a slow slip event beside a locked section of the offshore Kerran Fault. Varga's work therefore implies that the event ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: will trigger a large earthquake on the locked section within weeks
released stress that had built up on the fault's locked section
made the Kerran Fault more hazardous than any other offshore fault
may have made a large earthquake on the locked section more likely
items.explanation: The shared term is stress on the locked section. Slow slip can add that stress, and added stress raises the chance of rupture. So the 2023 event may have raised the chance of a large earthquake. The words 'can' and 'chance' limit how strong the conclusion can be, which is why the answer says 'may have' and 'more likely.'

A.why: This is strength creep. The passage supports a higher chance of an earthquake, not a certain one within a set time.

B.why: You reversed the relationship. The passage says slow slip shifts stress onto locked sections, not that it relieves their stress.

items.subtype_name: Chained percents across several quantities
items.stimulus: An ecologist surveying three ponds found that the frog population of Pond A is 25% greater than the frog population of Pond B, and the frog population of Pond B is 20% less than the frog population of Pond C. Pond C has 480 frogs.
items.stem: How many frogs live in Pond A?
items.explanation: Work through the chain one multiplier at a time. Pond B is 20% less than Pond C, so $B = 0.8(480) = 384$. Pond A is 25% greater than Pond B, so $A = 1.25(384) = 480$. C.why: You added the percents, +25% − 20% = +5%, and computed $1.05(480) = 504$. Successive percent changes multiply. They do not add.

D.why: You got $B = 384$ correctly but then applied the 25% to the wrong base. You treated B as 25% less than A and computed $A = 384 / 0.75 = 512$. The base is the quantity after 'than', which is Pond B, so $A = 1.25B$.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse spends its days picking parasites off larger reef fish. Because of this, marine biologists long assumed that the wrasse's clients put up with it purely for that service. ______, a field study led by marine biologist Tomasz Rehak found that client fish kept visiting cleaning stations just as often after divers had already removed all of their parasites. The finding suggests that the fish seek out the wrasse's touch for its own sake.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first part sets up a long-held assumption: clients tolerate the wrasse only because it removes parasites. The study then shows that clients keep coming even when there are no parasites left to remove, which undercuts that assumption. A sentence that overturns an expectation needs a contrast word, and 'However' is the only contrast word among the choices.

A.why: You saw that both sentences are about why clients visit the wrasse and never checked which way the logic runs. The assumption doesn't cause the study's result. The result goes against it.

B.why: 'Similarly' says the second sentence matches the first. The study contradicts the assumption instead of repeating it.

D.why: 'For instance' would make the study one example of the belief that clients come only for parasite removal. The study is evidence against that belief, not an example of it.

items.stimulus: Adding a lane to a congested highway would seem, on its face, to ______ traffic on that route. Transportation researchers have repeatedly found the counterintuitive reverse: within a few years of a widening, the new capacity draws in enough additional drivers that congestion returns to its former level or even worsens.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: "Would seem" and "counterintuitive reverse" tell you the blank holds the common expectation that research overturns. The finding is that congestion "returns to its former level" or gets worse, so the expectation must be that a new lane eases congestion. "Relieve" fits the claim that congestion gets lighter, with no more certainty than that.

A.why: You missed what "counterintuitive" signals. "Intensify" describes the research finding, not the expectation it overturns. Nobody expects a new lane to make traffic worse.

B.why: You chose the right direction but a claim that is too strong. Nobody reasonably expects one extra lane to get rid of traffic altogether. The finding is framed against the expectation of lighter congestion, not zero congestion.

C.why: You picked a traffic-engineering word that fits the topic but not the logic. Widening a road does not send traffic elsewhere, and "reroute" has no link to congestion returning or worsening.

items.subtype_name: Similar / congruent figures: read off corresponding parts
items.stimulus: A hydrologist studies a drainage channel whose cross-section is triangle $ABC$, with the lowest point $C$ at the bottom and the rim $\overline{AB}$ at ground level. The rim is 8 meters wide, and the channel is 5 meters deep, measured along the altitude from $C$ to $\overline{AB}$. During a storm, the water surface forms segment $\overline{DE}$, with $D$ on $\overline{CA}$ and $E$ on $\overline{CB}$. $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and is 6 meters wide.
items.stem: What is the depth, in meters, of the water at the center of the channel?
items.explanation: Because $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{AB}$, triangle $CDE$ is similar to triangle $CAB$, so corresponding altitudes are in the same ratio as corresponding sides. The water depth $d$ is the altitude of the small triangle, so $\frac{d}{5} = \frac{6}{8}$ and $d = \frac{30}{8} = \frac{15}{4}$ meters.

A.why: You found the height of the dry part of the channel, $5 - \frac{15}{4} = \frac{5}{4}$. The water depth is the altitude of the small triangle below the surface.

B.why: The surface is 2 meters narrower than the rim, so you subtracted 2 meters from the depth. Similar triangles shrink by a common factor, not by a common amount.

D.why: You wrote $\frac{d}{5} = \frac{8}{6}$, which puts the large triangle's width over the small one's. That gives a depth greater than the channel itself.

In most metals, shrinking the crystal grains raises hardness, because the boundaries between grains block the dislocations that let a metal deform. Materials scientist Hye-jin Park suspected that this effect has a limit. When grains become extremely small, she reasoned, the boundaries themselves begin to slide, and hardness should drop. Q | 80 | 4.4
R | 35 | 5.6

the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.

items.stimulus:
Winter cover crops such as cereal rye are planted after harvest and killed in spring, which leaves a layer of residue on the soil surface. That residue slows evaporation, so the soil under it holds more water into midsummer, when corn is most sensitive to moisture stress. Agronomists at a Nebraska research farm compared corn grown after rye with corn grown on bare soil over eight seasons, four wet and four dry. They concluded that a rye cover crop raises corn yields in dry seasons, when the extra stored water matters most.

Average Corn Yield (bushels per acre)
Season type | Bare soil | After rye
Wet | 182 | 176
Dry | 131 | 154
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the agronomists' conclusion?
choices: In wet seasons, corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre, while corn grown after rye yielded 176.
Corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre in wet seasons but only 131 bushels per acre in dry seasons.
In dry seasons, corn grown after rye yielded 154 bushels per acre, while corn grown on bare soil yielded 131.
Corn grown after rye yielded more per acre than corn grown on bare soil in both wet seasons and dry seasons.
items.explanation: The conclusion is limited to dry seasons and compares rye with bare soil. So you need the dry row, with rye higher than bare soil. Choice C gives exactly that: 154 bushels against 131.

A.why: You ignored the condition the claim depends on. The conclusion is about dry seasons, and this choice reports only the wet row. In that row rye doesn't even raise yields.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice holds the treatment fixed at bare soil and compares weather conditions. That shows drought lowers yield, not that rye raises it.

D.why: You misread the wet row. In wet seasons corn after rye yielded 176 bushels, less than the 182 bushels on bare soil.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into the soft sediments that fill many valleys, they slow down and grow in amplitude, so the ground shakes harder. Seismologists express this as an amplification factor: peak shaking at a sediment site divided by peak shaking at a nearby bedrock site. Distant earthquakes arrive dominated by long-period waves, which sediment layers tend to resonate with. For that reason, one team hypothesized that basin sediments amplify shaking from distant earthquakes more than shaking from nearby ones.

Average Peak Ground Acceleration (cm/s²)
Earthquake distance | Bedrock sites | Sediment sites
Under 50 km | 120 | 180
Over 150 km | 20 | 50
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
choices: For nearby earthquakes, sediment sites exceeded bedrock sites by 60 cm/s², whereas for distant ones the gap was only 30 cm/s².
Sediment sites recorded stronger shaking than bedrock sites did for both nearby earthquakes and distant earthquakes.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for nearby earthquakes but 1.5 times for distant ones.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for distant earthquakes but 1.5 times for nearby ones.
items.explanation: The passage defines amplification as a ratio, sediment divided by bedrock. So you have to compute it: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 for distant earthquakes and 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5 for nearby ones. Choice D shows that distant earthquakes are amplified more, which is what the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw differences when the passage defined amplification as a ratio. The gaps are accurate, but subtraction doesn't measure the amplification factor. Measured as a ratio, the result goes the other way.

B.why: You chose a true statement that supports a broader claim, that sediments amplify shaking at all. The hypothesis is about which distance is amplified more, and this choice doesn't compare the two.

C.why: You reversed the ratios. Nearby earthquakes give 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5, and distant ones give 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, not the other way around.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Hillshading simulates the shadows that terrain casts under light from one direction. It is often added to contour maps to make relief easier to see. Cartographer Tomasz Wierzbicki asked novice and experienced map readers to identify the easiest walking routes on contour-only or hillshaded versions of the same maps. Experienced readers can already picture terrain from contour lines alone. Wierzbicki therefore hypothesized that hillshading would improve novices' accuracy more than it would improve experienced readers' accuracy.

Route Choices Judged Correct (%)
Reader group | Contour-only map | Hillshaded map
Novice | 58 | 64
Experienced | 71 | 83
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken Wierzbicki's hypothesis?
choices: Hillshading raised experienced readers' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised novices' accuracy by only 6 points.
Novices chose correct routes 64% of the time with hillshaded maps and 58% of the time with contour-only maps.
Experienced readers chose correct routes more often than novices did with both contour-only and hillshaded maps.
Hillshading raised novices' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised experienced readers' accuracy by only 6 points.
items.explanation: The hypothesis predicts that the novices' gain from hillshading will be larger than the experienced readers' gain. To weaken it, you need the opposite. Experienced readers gained 12 points (71 to 83), and novices gained only 6 (58 to 64). Choice A states that.

B.why: You stopped at one group. This choice shows that novices improved, but the hypothesis compares the size of the improvement across both groups. A single row can't weaken that comparison.

C.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice compares reader groups within each map type. The hypothesis is about how much hillshading changes each group's accuracy.

D.why: You swapped the rows. Novices gained 6 points and experienced readers gained 12. Also, the reversed version would support the hypothesis, not weaken it.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Economists who study employee turnover often find that workers leave jobs when their schedules clash with obligations outside work. A logistics firm let some of its office staff work remotely while others remained on-site. Analysts tracked who quit over the following year and separated employees who reported caring for a child or relative from those who did not. The analysts concluded that remote eligibility lowers quit rates among caregivers but has little effect on employees without caregiving duties.

Annual Quit Rate (%)
Employee group | On-site | Remote-eligible
Caregivers | 18 | 9
Non-caregivers | 11 | 10
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analysts' conclusion?
choices: Remote-eligible caregivers quit at a rate of 9%, half the 18% rate among caregivers who remained on-site.
Among on-site employees, caregivers quit at a rate of 18%, while non-caregivers quit at a rate of 11%.
Remote-eligible non-caregivers quit at a rate of 10%, well below the 18% rate among on-site non-caregivers.
Remote eligibility cut caregivers' quit rate from 18% to 9% but changed non-caregivers' rate only from 11% to 10%.
items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: a large drop for caregivers and little change for non-caregivers. Choice D covers both. Caregivers' quit rate fell from 18% to 9%, and non-caregivers' barely moved, from 11% to 10%.

A.why: You supported only half of the conclusion. This choice shows the drop for caregivers but says nothing about the claim that remote work has little effect on non-caregivers.

B.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice holds work arrangement fixed at on-site and compares the two employee groups, so it doesn't show any effect of remote eligibility.

C.why: You read across into the wrong row. On-site non-caregivers quit at 11%, not 18%. The 18% figure belongs to on-site caregivers.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Vaccine adjuvants are added to stimulate the innate immune cells that help launch an antibody response, and these cells become less responsive with age. Researchers gave younger and older adults a flu vaccine with or without an experimental adjuvant. They measured antibody titers before vaccination and four weeks after. Because baseline titers differ by age, they compared groups using the fold rise: the post-vaccination titer divided by the pre-vaccination titer. They hypothesized that the adjuvant would benefit older adults more than younger adults.

Mean Antibody Titer
Group | Pre-vaccination | Post-vaccination
Younger, standard vaccine | 50 | 400
Younger, with adjuvant | 50 | 500
Older, standard vaccine | 10 | 30
Older, with adjuvant | 10 | 90
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: The adjuvant raised younger adults' post-vaccination titer by 100, compared with a rise of only 60 for older adults.
The adjuvant raised older adults' fold rise from 3 to 9 but raised younger adults' fold rise only from 8 to 10.
Older adults given the adjuvant reached a titer of 90, three times the 30 reached with the standard vaccine.
Older adults given the adjuvant showed a larger fold rise than younger adults given the same adjuvant did.
items.explanation: The researchers measure benefit using fold rise, so you have to compute it for all four rows. For older adults, fold rise went from 3 (30 ÷ 10) to 9 (90 ÷ 10). For younger adults, it went from 8 (400 ÷ 50) to 10 (500 ÷ 50). Older adults gained far more, as the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw titers when the passage said groups are compared by fold rise. The differences of 100 and 60 are accurate. But because baselines differ so much, raw gains don't measure the benefit the researchers defined.

C.why: You stopped at one age group. This choice shows the adjuvant helped older adults, but the hypothesis claims they benefit more than younger adults. That requires the younger adults' data too.

D.why: You misread the adjuvant rows. With the adjuvant, older adults' fold rise was 9 and younger adults' was 10, so older adults' fold rise was not larger. The hypothesis concerns the size of the gain, not the final fold rise.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
In a highly reverberant building, each note an organ plays lingers for several seconds, and rapid passages can blur into an indistinct wash. Musicologist Inês Carvalho compared recordings of the same organists performing in acoustically dry churches and in reverberant cathedrals. She reasoned that because blurring is worst when notes follow one another quickly, players would compensate by slowing down. She claimed that reverberation reduces tempo more in fast pieces than in slow ones.

Average Tempo (beats per minute)
Piece type | Dry church | Reverberant cathedral
Fast | 132 | 112
Slow | 64 | 60
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Carvalho's claim?
choices: Organists slowed fast pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed slow pieces by only 4.
Organists played both fast and slow pieces at lower tempos in reverberant cathedrals than in dry churches.
In reverberant cathedrals, organists played fast pieces at 112 beats per minute and slow pieces at 60.
Organists slowed slow pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed fast pieces by only 4.
items.explanation: Carvalho's claim compares the size of the slowdown in the two kinds of piece. Fast pieces dropped from 132 to 112, a fall of 20 beats per minute. Slow pieces dropped from 64 to 60, a fall of 4. Choice A makes that comparison.

B.why: You chose an accurate statement that supports a weaker claim, that reverberation slows tempo in general. Carvalho claims the effect is larger for fast pieces, and this choice doesn't compare the size of the two slowdowns.

C.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice compares fast and slow pieces within the cathedral column. Fast pieces are faster everywhere, so this says nothing about the effect of reverberation.

D.why: You swapped the rows. Fast pieces lost 20 beats per minute and slow pieces lost 4, not the reverse.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Adding clay platelets a few nanometers thick to a polymer can stiffen it by restricting how freely its molecular chains slide past one another. This restriction was thought to matter mainly above the polymer's softening point, where the chains move most freely. A materials team tested an epoxy with and without 5% nanoclay at 25°C and at 120°C, a temperature above its softening point. The team hypothesized that nanoclay improves the epoxy's stiffness only at temperatures above that point.

Stiffness (gigapascals)
Test temperature | Without nanoclay | With nanoclay
25°C | 2.4 | 3.1
120°C | 0.6 | 1.4
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken the team's hypothesis?
choices: At 120°C, the epoxy with nanoclay had a stiffness of 1.4 gigapascals, compared with 0.6 without it.
Both versions of the epoxy were stiffer at 25°C than at 120°C, with or without the added nanoclay.
At 25°C, the epoxy with nanoclay had a stiffness of 3.1 gigapascals, compared with 2.4 without it.
At 25°C, the epoxy without nanoclay had a stiffness of 3.1 gigapascals, compared with 2.4 with it.
items.explanation: The word 'only' is what you need to test. If nanoclay helps only above the softening point, it should make no difference at 25°C. Instead, it raised stiffness from 2.4 to 3.1 gigapascals at 25°C, which undercuts the hypothesis.

A.why: You chose the condition where the hypothesis predicts a benefit. An improvement at 120°C fits the hypothesis, so it can't weaken it. The claim is vulnerable only at the lower temperature.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice compares temperatures within each material. The hypothesis is about the effect of nanoclay at each temperature.

D.why: You swapped the columns. At 25°C, the epoxy with nanoclay measured 3.1 and the one without measured 2.4. The reversed version would actually support the hypothesis.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
In many songbirds, both parents carry insects to the nest, and a larger brood means more hungry mouths per trip. Ecologists watching blue tit nests counted parents' feeding visits per hour at broods of three and of six chicks. They made counts in a year when caterpillars were plentiful and in a year when a late frost made them scarce. They measured provisioning as visits per chick: hourly visits divided by brood size. They concluded that when food is scarce, chicks in large broods are fed less often than chicks in small broods.

Parental Feeding Visits per Hour
Year | Brood of three | Brood of six
Plentiful caterpillars | 12 | 24
Scarce caterpillars | 12 | 15
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologists' conclusion?
choices: In the scarce year, parents of six-chick broods made 15 visits per hour, more than the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the scarce year, chicks in broods of six received 2.5 visits each per hour, while chicks in broods of three received 4.
In the plentiful year, parents of six-chick broods made 24 visits per hour, twice the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the plentiful year, chicks in broods of six received fewer visits each per hour than chicks in broods of three did.
items.explanation: The conclusion applies to the scarce year and depends on visits per chick, so you have to divide. In the scarce year, 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 visits per chick in large broods and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 in small broods. Chicks in large broods were fed less often, as the ecologists concluded.

A.why: You used raw hourly visits when the ecologists defined provisioning per chick. Large-brood parents made more total visits, but those visits were shared among twice as many chicks.

C.why: You ignored the condition the claim depends on. The conclusion concerns the year when food was scarce, and this choice reports the plentiful year using raw totals instead of visits per chick.

D.why: You misread the plentiful year. Chicks in both brood sizes received 4 visits each per hour (24 ÷ 6 and 12 ÷ 3), so large-brood chicks did not receive fewer.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: On a regional map, the scale is 1 centimeter = 5 kilometers. On the map, a rural region covers an area of 12 square centimeters. The region has a population of 24,000 people.
items.stem: What is the population density, in people per square kilometer, of the region?
items.explanation: Area scales by the square of the length scale. Each square centimeter on the map is $5 \text{ km} \times 5 \text{ km} = 25$ square kilometers, so the real area is $12 \times 25 = 300$ square kilometers. Density is people ÷ area: $\frac{24{,}000}{300} = 80$ people per square kilometer.

A.why: You flipped the quotient and divided area by population, $\frac{300}{24{,}000} = 0.0125$. That is square kilometers per person, not people per square kilometer.

C.why: You converted the area with the length scale instead of its square: $12 \times 5 = 60$ square kilometers, which gives $\frac{24{,}000}{60} = 400$. A square centimeter on the map is 5 km by 5 km, so it stands for 25 square kilometers.

D.why: You divided the population by the map area, $\frac{24{,}000}{12} = 2{,}000$, and never converted the 12 square centimeters to real square kilometers.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: A planetary scientist makes a scale model of a rocky asteroid fragment. The model is a solid cube with a mass of 24,000 grams, made from a material with a density of 3 grams per cubic centimeter.
items.stem: What is the edge length, in centimeters, of the cube?
items.explanation: Volume = mass ÷ density $= \frac{24{,}000 \text{ g}}{3 \text{ g/cm}^3} = 8{,}000$ cubic centimeters. For a cube, the edge length is the cube root of the volume: $\sqrt[3]{8{,}000} = 20$ centimeters.

A.why: You divided density by mass, $\frac{3}{24{,}000} = \frac{1}{8{,}000}$, and took the cube root to get $0.05$. The units show the error: g/cm³ ÷ g does not give cubic centimeters.

C.why: You found the volume of 8,000 cubic centimeters and then divided it by 3 instead of taking the cube root. The edge of a cube is $\sqrt[3]{V}$, not $\frac{V}{3}$.

D.why: 8,000 is the cube's volume in cubic centimeters. The question asks for the edge length, so you still have to take the cube root.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: Folklorists surveying a river valley recorded 1,260 distinct local legends. Their report gives a density of 9 recorded legends per square kilometer of inhabited land. The valley region also contains a 40-square-kilometer reservoir, which is uninhabited and is not counted as inhabited land.
items.stem: What is the total area, in square kilometers, of the valley region?
items.explanation: Work backward from the density: inhabited area = legends ÷ density $= \frac{1{,}260}{9} = 140$ square kilometers. The total region also includes the reservoir, so the total area is $140 + 40 = 180$ square kilometers.

A.why: You subtracted the reservoir, $140 - 40 = 100$, when you should have added it. The 140 square kilometers already leaves out the reservoir, so the total area is larger than 140.

B.why: 140 square kilometers is only the inhabited land. You stopped before adding the 40-square-kilometer reservoir to get the total area the question asks for.

D.why: You multiplied the count by the density, $1{,}260 \times 9 = 11{,}340$, and then added 40. To go from a density back to an area, divide the amount by the density.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: A civil engineer designs a solid concrete footing shaped like a rectangular prism with a square base and a height of 0.5 meter. The footing has a mass of 4,800 kilograms, and the concrete has a density of 2,400 kilograms per cubic meter.
items.stem: What is the side length, in meters, of the footing's square base?
items.explanation: Volume = mass ÷ density $= \frac{4{,}800}{2{,}400} = 2$ cubic meters. Divide by the height to get the base area: $\frac{2}{0.5} = 4$ square meters. The side of the square base is $\sqrt{4} = 2$ meters.

A.why: You divided density by mass, $\frac{2{,}400}{4{,}800} = 0.5$, and treated that as the volume. That gives a base area of 1 square meter and a side of 1 meter. Volume is mass ÷ density.

B.why: You took the square root of the volume, 2 cubic meters, as if it were the base area. You ignored the 0.5-meter height, which you need to divide out before taking the square root.

D.why: 4 is the area of the base in square meters. The question asks for the side length, so take its square root.

items.stimulus: A sports scientist estimates an athlete's body composition by underwater weighing. The athlete has a mass of 78 kilograms. items.stem: Which of the following is closest to the athlete's body density, in kilograms per liter?

items.explanation: Strikes per square kilometer over the full period: $\frac{5{,}400}{600} = 9$. Divide by the 3 years to get a yearly rate: $\frac{9}{3} = 3$ strikes per square kilometer per year.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
While checking a pressure-correction step, a meteorology student arrives at the equation below.

$\frac{1}{2}(x+3)^2 - 8 = 10$
items.stem: What are the solutions to the given equation?
items.explanation: Add 8 to both sides to get $\frac{1}{2}(x+3)^2 = 18$. Multiply by 2 to get $(x+3)^2 = 36$. Then $x+3 = 6$ or $x+3 = -6$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -9$.

A.why: You took only the positive square root, $x+3 = 6$. You forgot that $x+3 = -6$ also works, which gives the second solution, $x = -9$.

B.why: You divided 18 by 2 when you should have multiplied, so you got $(x+3)^2 = 9$. That gives $x+3 = \pm 3$, so $x = 0$ or $x = -6$.

D.why: You found $x+3 = \pm 6$ correctly but flipped the sign of 3 when you isolated $x$. You wrote $x = 3 \pm 6$ when it should be $x = -3 \pm 6$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An ecologist modelling how a pond's algae cover recovers after treatment reduces one step to the equation below.

$x^2 = 6x + 11$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Rewrite the equation in standard form as $x^2 - 6x - 11 = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36+44}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 4\sqrt{5}}{2} = 3 \pm 2\sqrt{5}$. Since $2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.47$, only $3+2\sqrt{5}$ is positive.

A.why: You kept the sign of $6x$ when you moved it to the left side, so you solved $x^2 + 6x - 11 = 0$. The roots of that equation are $-3 \pm 2\sqrt{5}$, which is a different equation.

B.why: This is a root of the equation, but $2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.47$ is larger than 3, so $3-2\sqrt{5}$ is negative. The question asks for the positive solution.

C.why: You divided only the radical part of $\frac{6+4\sqrt{5}}{2}$ by 2. The 6 has to be divided by 2 as well, which gives 3.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:

$(x-4)(x+2) = 2x + 7$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Expand the left side to get $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 2x + 7$, which becomes $x^2 - 4x - 15 = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16+60}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{19}$. Only $2+\sqrt{19}$ is positive.

A.why: You expanded the middle term as $+2x$ when it should be $-2x$. The $x$ terms then cancelled and you were left with $x^2 = 15$.

B.why: You added 7 when you moved it to the left side, so you solved $x^2 - 4x - 1 = 0$. The correct step subtracts 7, which gives $-15$.

items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$ for the linear function $f$. If $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b$?
items.explanation: Take the slope from any two rows: $\frac{31 - 19}{5 - 2} = \frac{12}{3} = 4$, so $a = 4$. Put the point $(2, 19)$ into $f(x) = 4x + b$: $19 = 8 + b$, so $b = 11$. The rows $(5, 31)$ and $(9, 47)$ also fit $f(x) = 4x + 11$. The question asks for $a + b$, which is $4 + 11 = 15$.

D.why: You took the first row's output, 19, as the $y$-intercept. That row is at $x = 2$, not $x = 0$, so 19 is not $b$. Adding it to the slope of 4 gives 23.

items.stimulus: A wetland ecologist models the number of breeding pairs of a marsh bird in a protected reserve, $y$, as a linear function of $x$, the number of years after 2010. According to the model, there were 62 breeding pairs when $x = 4$ and 44 breeding pairs when $x = 10$.
items.stem: Which equation represents this relationship?
items.explanation: The two data points are $(4, 62)$ and $(10, 44)$. The slope is $\frac{44 - 62}{10 - 4} = \frac{-18}{6} = -3$. That makes sense, because the population is going down. B.why: This line goes through $(10, 44)$, but at $x = 4$ it gives 56, not 62. An equation has to fit both given points, not just one.

C.why: You used 62 as the $y$-intercept. That is the count at $x = 4$, not at $x = 0$, so it is not the value of $b$.

items.stimulus: In a digestion study, nutrition scientists model the percent of a test meal's starch still present in the stomach with the linear function $p$, where $x$ is the number of minutes since the first measurement.
items.stem: The graph of the linear function $p$ in the xy-plane has a slope of $-3$ and passes through the point $(12, 40)$. Which equation defines $p$?
items.explanation: Substitute the point into $p(x) = -3x + b$: $40 = -3(12) + b = -36 + b$, so $b = 76$. That gives $p(x) = -3x + 76$.

A.why: This line goes through $(12, 40)$, but its slope is $+3$, not $-3$. You dropped the negative sign, so your model has the starch increasing when it should be decreasing.

C.why: You used 40 as the y-intercept. But 40 is the value when $x = 12$, not when $x = 0$.

D.why: You subtracted 36 from 40 instead of adding it. From $40 = -36 + b$, you get $b = 76$.

items.subtype_name: Build the line from two points, a table, or slope plus a point
items.stimulus: A printmaker models the total time, in minutes, needed to pull $x$ prints from an inked linocut block with the linear function $f$. The time includes a fixed setup period.
items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The graph of $y = f(x)$ in the xy-plane passes through the points $(3, 17)$ and $(7, 29)$. What is the value of $ab$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{29 - 17}{7 - 3} = \frac{12}{4} = 3$, so $a = 3$. Substitute $(3, 17)$: $17 = 9 + b$, so $b = 8$. The question asks for the product, so $ab = 3 \times 8 = 24$.

A.why: You computed the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$. That gives $b = 16$ and $ab = \frac{16}{3}$. Slope is the change in output divided by the change in input.

B.why: 8 is $b$, the setup time. The question asks for $ab$, so you still have to multiply by the slope, 3.

C.why: 11 is $a + b$. You found both constants correctly, but the question asks for their product, not their sum.

items.stimulus: A musicologist transcribing a set of village dance tunes uses a function $f$ to estimate how many measures a tune contains when it has $x$ repeated phrases.
items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 3x + 6$. What is the value of $f(12)$?

A.why: You solved $3x + 6 = 12$ and got $x = 2$. The question asks for $f(12)$, the output when the input is 12, not the input that gives an output of 12.

B.why: You multiplied $3 \times 12$ and stopped there. You still need to add the constant 6.

D.why: You added 12 and 6 first and then multiplied by 3, which gives $3(18) = 54$. In order of operations, you multiply $3 \times 12$ before adding 6.

items.subtype_name: Plug in and evaluate
items.stimulus: An archaeologist labels soil layers by their position relative to a reference marker, and layers below the marker get negative numbers. A function $g$ gives the estimated age, in centuries, of the layer at position $x$.
items.stem: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x) = -2x + 8$. What is the value of $g(-4)$?
items.explanation: Put $-4$ in for $x$ and keep the parentheses: $g(-4) = -2(-4) + 8 = 8 + 8 = 16$.

A.why: You dropped the negative sign on the input and calculated $-2(4) + 8 = 0$. A negative times a negative is positive, so $-2(-4) = 8$.

B.why: You left out the parentheses around $-4$ and read $-2 - 4 + 8$, which is 2. You should have multiplied $-2$ by $-4$.

C.why: You solved $-2x + 8 = -4$ and got $x = 6$. The question asks for the output $g(-4)$, not the input that makes the output equal $-4$.

items.subtype_name: Plug in or solve for the input
items.stimulus: An immunologist models the concentration of a certain antibody in a patient's blood after the concentration peaks. The function $C$ is defined by $C(t) = 640\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5}$, where $C(t)$ is the concentration, in units per milliliter, $t$ days after the peak.
items.stem: For what value of $t$ does $C(t) = 40$?

items.stimulus: An archaeologist models the cross-section of a burial mound. The function $h$ is defined by $h(x) = 18 - \frac{1}{8}(x - 12)^2$, where $h(x)$ is the height of the mound, in meters, at a horizontal distance of $x$ meters from the mound's western edge, for $0 \le x \le 24$.
items.stem: For what value of $x$, where $x < 12$, does $h(x) = 10$?
items.explanation: Set $18 - \frac{1}{8}(x - 12)^2 = 10$. Subtract 18 to get $-\frac{1}{8}(x - 12)^2 = -8$, then multiply by $-8$ to get $(x - 12)^2 = 64$. So $x - 12 = 8$ or $x - 12 = -8$, which means $x = 20$ or $x = 4$. Only $x = 4$ meets the condition $x < 12$.

B.why: 8 is the square root of 64, so it is the distance $|x - 12|$ from the center. You still need to add or subtract it from 12 to get $x$.

C.why: You found $h(10)$, the height at a distance of 10 meters, instead of the distance at which the height is 10 meters. You swapped the input and the output.

D.why: 20 does solve $h(x) = 10$, but it fails the condition $x < 12$. You took only the positive square root and missed the solution from the negative root.

items.stimulus: A hydrologist estimates the flow of water over a small weir using the function $Q$, defined by $Q(h) = 3h^{3/2}$, where $Q(h)$ is the flow rate, in liters per second, when the water stands $h$ centimeters above the crest of the weir.
items.stem: For what value of $h$ does $Q(h) = 81$?

D.why: You calculated $Q(81)$, the flow rate when the height is 81, instead of the height that gives a flow rate of 81. You swapped the input and the output.

items.stimulus: In equal-tempered tuning, the frequency of a pitch depends on how many half steps it is from a reference pitch. The function $f$ is defined by $f(n) = 440 \cdot 2^{n/12}$, where $f(n)$ is the frequency, in hertz, of the pitch that is $n$ half steps above the reference pitch. A negative $n$ means the pitch is below the reference pitch.
items.stem: For what value of $n$ does $f(n) = 55$?
items.explanation: Set $440 \cdot 2^{n/12} = 55$ and divide by 440 to get $2^{n/12} = \frac{1}{8} = 2^{-3}$. So $\frac{n}{12} = -3$, which gives $n = -36$. This makes sense because 55 hertz is lower than 440 hertz, so the pitch has to be below the reference.

B.why: $-3$ is the value of the exponent $\frac{n}{12}$. You still need to multiply by 12 to get $n$.

C.why: You set the exponent $\frac{n}{12}$ equal to $\frac{1}{8}$ itself instead of the power of 2 that equals $\frac{1}{8}$. Since $\frac{1}{8} = 2^{-3}$, the exponent must be $-3$.

D.why: You dropped the negative sign. $\frac{1}{8}$ is $2^{-3}$, not $2^3$, and a frequency below 440 hertz has to come from a negative $n$.

items.subtype_name: Plug in or solve for the input
items.stimulus: A materials scientist heats a metal alloy and tracks the growth of its crystal grains. The function $g$ is defined by $g(t) = 4\sqrt[3]{t - 3} + 1$, where $g(t)$ is the average grain diameter, in micrometers, $t$ minutes after heating begins, for $t \ge 3$.
items.stem: For what value of $t$ does $g(t) = 9$?
items.explanation: Set $4\sqrt[3]{t - 3} + 1 = 9$ and undo the operations in reverse order. Subtract 1: $4\sqrt[3]{t - 3} = 8$. Divide by 4: $\sqrt[3]{t - 3} = 2$. Cube both sides: $t - 3 = 8$. Add 3: $t = 11$. Check: $g(11) = 4(2) + 1 = 9$.

A.why: You found that $\sqrt[3]{t - 3} = 2$ but then set $t - 3 = 2$ without cubing. To remove a cube root, you have to cube both sides.

B.why: 8 is the value of $t - 3$. You still need to add 3 to get $t$.

D.why: You cubed 8 before dividing by the coefficient 4. When you work backward, divide by 4 first so that the cube root is on its own, and only then cube.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Because slow slip events release built-up strain gradually, over days or weeks and without violent shaking, many seismologists long regarded them as a kind of safety valve for faults. Geophysicist Tomasz Rydel's analysis of two decades of GPS data from a Pacific subduction zone, however, found that four of the region's six largest earthquakes struck within months of a slow slip event on a neighboring stretch of the fault. Each of those slip events appeared to have shifted strain onto the segment that later ruptured. Rydel's findings therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: slow slip events lower the likelihood of a major earthquake on a fault.
slow slip events can move strain from one section of a fault to another.
most major subduction earthquakes are triggered by earlier slow slip events.
GPS measurements can detect fault slip that produces no violent shaking.
items.explanation: The old view is the 'safety valve' idea: by releasing strain quietly, slow slip events make large earthquakes less likely. Rydel found that most of the biggest quakes came soon after slow slip events that loaded strain onto the segment that then ruptured. That attacks the safety-valve reasoning directly, so the doubted idea is that slow slip lowers the chance of a major earthquake.

B.why: You picked what Rydel's data support, not what they undercut. The strain shifting between segments is the new finding, on the far side of the 'however'. It is not the old view being doubted.

C.why: You made the study's claim bigger than it is. Four quakes in one subduction zone can't show that most subduction earthquakes everywhere are triggered this way, and nothing here is doubted in any case.

D.why: You latched onto a detail of the method. Rydel's study depends on GPS picking up quiet slip, so it takes that ability for granted and doesn't question it.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Transportation agencies have long set weight limits on aging bridges on the premise that the repeated stress of heavy trucks is what chiefly wears down concrete decks. But when civil engineer Priya Nandakumar compared 212 bridges in a northern state, she found that decks carrying only light local traffic had deteriorated at nearly the same rate as decks on busy freight routes. In both groups, the damage tracked closely with the number of winters in which the deck had been treated with de-icing salt. Nandakumar's results challenge the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: de-icing salt harms concrete decks more than freezing temperatures do.
decks treated with de-icing salt tend to show greater deterioration.
heavy truck traffic is the main cause of wear on concrete decks.
bridges in northern states deteriorate faster than bridges elsewhere.
items.explanation: The old assumption behind weight limits is that heavy trucks are the main thing wearing decks down. If lightly used decks deteriorate about as fast as decks on freight routes, traffic load can't be the chief cause. So the challenged assumption is that heavy truck traffic is the main source of wear.

A.why: You claimed a comparison the study never made. Nandakumar linked damage to salt treatment but never measured salt against freezing temperatures on their own.

B.why: You chose the new finding instead of the old belief. The salt pattern is what Nandakumar's data support, so it can't be the assumption her results challenge.

D.why: You stretched the sample beyond where it came from. All 212 bridges were in one northern state, so the study says nothing about how they compare with bridges elsewhere.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: In classic planetarium experiments, caged migratory songbirds hopped toward the correct seasonal direction when shown a projected night sky, and ornithologists concluded that such birds rely primarily on the stars to steer. Recently, however, a team led by Ines Varga fitted 40 wild Swainson's thrushes with miniature radio tags. The researchers found that birds flying beneath complete cloud cover held their headings just as accurately as birds flying on clear nights. The team's results cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: thrushes rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field to steer at night.
night-migrating thrushes depend chiefly on the stars to steer.
thrushes can hold a steady heading without seeing the night sky.
caged songbirds orient correctly under projected star patterns.
items.explanation: The old conclusion was that these birds steer mainly by the stars. Thrushes that can't see any stars under full cloud cover still navigate as accurately as on clear nights, which undercuts the claim that stars are their main guide. The doubted idea is therefore that the thrushes depend chiefly on the stars.

A.why: You added a step the study never took. It showed that stars aren't needed, but it never tested magnetism, so it can't say what the birds use instead.

C.why: You picked what the radio-tag data show rather than what they undercut. That the birds navigate without the sky is the new evidence, on the far side of the 'however'.

D.why: You restated the old experiment's result, not the conclusion drawn from it. Varga's study doesn't dispute that caged birds oriented under a projected sky. It disputes the idea that stars are their main guide.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Flood models used by regional planners typically represent a restored wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume, which is why restoration is often promoted as a dependable way to lower downstream flood peaks. Hydrologist Kofi Mensah-Boateng's stream-gauge records from the Kessler Creek basin tell a more complicated story. While restored wetlands there did reduce peak flows during isolated storms, during a run of back-to-back storms the already saturated wetlands released runoff almost as quickly as the surrounding cropland. These records call into question the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: restored wetlands fail to lower peak flows during isolated storms.
saturated wetlands release runoff more quickly than dry ones do.
restored wetlands worsen flooding compared with nearby cropland.
a restored wetland can hold the same volume of water in every storm.
items.explanation: The models treat a wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume. The gauge records show that storage shrinks once the wetland is saturated from earlier storms. What they call into question is the fixed-capacity assumption: that a wetland holds the same amount of water in every storm.

A.why: You reversed the half of the finding that held steady. The passage says the wetlands did reduce peak flows during isolated storms.

B.why: You picked what the new records suggest, not the assumption they challenge. Saturation cutting a wetland's capacity is the new finding, not the old model's premise.

C.why: You pushed 'almost as quickly as' up to 'worse than'. At their weakest, saturated wetlands roughly matched cropland. They never did worse.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Surveys have repeatedly found that athletes who stretch before exercising report fewer injuries than those who do not, a pattern that has made the pre-workout stretch nearly universal advice. Surveys cannot show, though, whether stretching itself is responsible. When sports scientist Lena Okafor randomly assigned 1,400 recreational runners either to stretch before every run or to skip stretching for a season, injury rates in the two groups were nearly identical, although the stretchers said they felt looser on their runs. Okafor's trial therefore undermines the belief that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: stretching before a run raises a runner's risk of being injured.
runners who stretch are more cautious in their training overall.
stretching before a run lowers a runner's risk of being injured.
stretching before a run leaves runners feeling less stiff overall.
items.explanation: The widely held belief, built on survey data, is that stretching prevents injuries. Okafor randomly assigned runners to groups, which rules out the problem the surveys had, and found nearly identical injury rates. That undermines the belief that stretching before a run lowers injury risk.

A.why: You flipped the claim in the wrong direction. The trial found nearly identical injury rates, so stretching didn't raise the risk either.

B.why: You filled the gap with an explanation nobody tested. The passage says surveys can't prove cause, but it never says that stretchers are more cautious.

D.why: You picked a result the trial actually recorded. The stretchers did report feeling looser, so this is supported by the new evidence, not undermined.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Hail reports submitted to forecasters in one High Plains region have more than tripled since 1990, and some meteorologists have interpreted this rise as a sign that hailstorms there are growing more common. Meteorologist Dana Whitcomb examined three decades of radar data, which record hail-bearing storms whether or not anyone sees them, and found no change in how often such storms occurred. The jump in reports instead tracked the region's population growth and the spread of storm-spotting apps. Whitcomb's analysis casts doubt on the interpretation that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: hail-producing storms have become more frequent in the region.
more residents and new apps have led to more hail being reported.
storm-spotting apps alone explain the increase in hail reports.
radar measures the size of hailstones better than observers do.
items.explanation: The interpretation under attack is that the rise in reports means hailstorms are becoming more common. Radar, which counts hail storms whether or not anyone sees them, shows no change in how often they occur. So the doubted interpretation is that hail-producing storms have become more frequent.

B.why: You picked Whitcomb's alternative explanation, not the interpretation she casts doubt on. Population growth and apps are on the new-evidence side of the passage.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. The reports tracked both population and apps, so 'alone' claims more than the passage allows, and it is Whitcomb's side in any case.

D.why: You drifted to a side issue. The passage uses radar to count how often storms occur and says nothing about measuring hailstone size.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Because pollen cores from a nearby lake show a sharp drop in cereal pollen around the time the Neolithic village of Tell Varosh was deserted, archaeologists have long attributed its abandonment to a drought that ruined the village's harvests. Radiocarbon dating by archaeologist Samira Haddad's team, however, places that decline in cereal pollen roughly 150 years after the last households left the site. The new dates call into question the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Tell Varosh was occupied for about 150 years before it was abandoned.
farming near the site declined only after the villagers had departed.
the village was abandoned as a result of conflict with its neighbors.
failed harvests caused by drought drove the villagers from the site.
items.explanation: The old view rested on timing: cereal pollen fell as the village emptied, so drought-ruined harvests supposedly drove people out. Haddad's dates put the pollen decline 150 years after the village was already empty, so it can't have caused the abandonment. The doubted idea is that drought and failed harvests forced the villagers to leave.

A.why: You attached the number to the wrong thing. The 150 years is the gap between abandonment and the pollen decline, not how long the village was lived in.

B.why: You picked what the new dates suggest. A pollen drop after everyone left fits the new evidence, so it is not the idea being questioned.

C.why: You supplied a replacement cause the passage never mentions. Knocking out the drought explanation doesn't prove conflict, and nothing here is about warfare.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Studies of older adults have found that those who receive a flu shot are far less likely to die of any cause during winter than those who do not, and some officials have cited this gap as a measure of how many deaths the vaccine prevents. Epidemiologist Rafael Duarte noticed, however, that vaccinated seniors in his cohort also had markedly lower death rates in the weeks before influenza began circulating, when the vaccine could not yet have mattered. Duarte's observation casts doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: flu shots offer older adults no real protection against influenza.
the winter death-rate gap mainly reflects the vaccine's protection.
vaccinated seniors tend to be healthier than unvaccinated seniors.
vaccinated and unvaccinated seniors die at similar rates pre-season.
items.explanation: Officials treated the whole winter gap in death rates as the vaccine's doing. Duarte found the same gap before flu was even circulating, when the vaccine couldn't have been the reason. That points to some other difference between the groups, which casts doubt on the idea that the gap mainly reflects the vaccine's protection.

A.why: You fell for strength creep. Showing that the gap overstates the vaccine's benefit is not the same as showing the vaccine offers no protection at all.

C.why: You picked what Duarte's observation suggests, not the idea it casts doubt on. Better baseline health among vaccinated seniors is on the new-evidence side of the 'however'.

D.why: You reversed a stated detail. The passage says vaccinated seniors had markedly lower death rates before flu season, not similar ones.

items.subtype_name: Expand, distribute, combine like terms
items.stimulus: A folklore archivist estimates how many recorded folktales are in two regional collections. The archivist uses the expressions below, where $x$ is the number of field-recording trips made to each region.
items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(4x^2 + 3x - 5) - (x^2 - 2x + 6)$?
items.explanation: Apply the minus sign to every term in the second bracket: $4x^2 + 3x - 5 - x^2 + 2x - 6$. Then add like terms: $4x^2 - x^2 = 3x^2$, $3x + 2x = 5x$ and $-5 - 6 = -11$. That gives $3x^2 + 5x - 11$.

A.why: You applied the minus sign only to $x^2$ and left $-2x$ and $+6$ as they were, so you got $x$ and $+1$ where you should have $5x$ and $-11$.

B.why: You applied the minus sign to $-2x$ but not to $+6$, so you added the constant instead of subtracting it and got $+1$ where you should have $-11$.

D.why: You added the two polynomials instead of subtracting the second from the first, so you found the sum, not the difference.

items.stimulus: In a field trial, an agronomist models the yield of two plots of a drought-tolerant sorghum variety with the expressions $P = 3x(2x - 5)$ and $Q = 4(x^2 + 2x)$, where $x$ is the number of irrigation cycles.
items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $P + Q$?
items.explanation: Distribute: $P = 6x^2 - 15x$ and $Q = 4x^2 + 8x$. Add like terms: $6x^2 + 4x^2 = 10x^2$ and $-15x + 8x = -7x$. So $P + Q = 10x^2 - 7x$.

A.why: When you combined $6x^2$ and $4x^2$ you added the exponents as well as the coefficients. When you combine like terms, only the coefficients change and the exponent stays 2.

C.why: You subtracted $Q$ from $P$ instead of adding them, so you found $P - Q$.

D.why: You combined $-15x$ and $+8x$ as if both were negative. $-15x + 8x$ is $-7x$, not $-23x$.

items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(x^2 - 3x + 8) + 2(x^2 + 4x - 1)$?
items.explanation: Multiply every term in the second bracket by 2: $2x^2 + 8x - 2$. Then add like terms: $x^2 + 2x^2 = 3x^2$, $-3x + 8x = 5x$ and $8 - 2 = 6$. That gives $3x^2 + 5x + 6$.

A.why: You multiplied only $x^2$ by 2 and left $4x$ and $-1$ undoubled, so you got $x$ and $7$ where you should have $5x$ and $6$.

B.why: You doubled $x^2$ and $4x$ but not the constant $-1$, so you got $+7$ instead of $+6$.

C.why: You treated $-3x$ as $+3x$ and added it to $8x$, getting $11x$ instead of $5x$.

items.subtype_name: Find the unknown constants from given points
items.stimulus: A meteorologist uses the function $P$ to estimate atmospheric pressure, in hectopascals (hPa), at an altitude of $h$ kilometers above sea level over a particular weather station. According to the model, the pressure is 900 hPa at an altitude of 1 kilometer and 729 hPa at an altitude of 3 kilometers.
items.stem: The function $P$ is defined by $P(h) = a \cdot b^h$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. What is the value of $a$?
items.explanation: Divide the two conditions: $\frac{a \cdot b^3}{a \cdot b^1} = \frac{729}{900}$, so $b^2 = 0.81$ and $b = 0.9$. Then $a \cdot 0.9 = 900$, so $a = 1{,}000$. This is the modeled pressure at sea level, where $h = 0$.

A.why: 0.9 is the value of $b$, the multiplier per kilometer. The question asks for $a$, the starting value.

B.why: You treated the pressure at $h = 1$ as the starting value. But $a$ is the value at $h = 0$, so you have to undo one factor of $b$: $900 \div 0.9 = 1{,}000$.

C.why: You assumed the pressure drops by the same amount each kilometer, $171 \div 2 = 85.5$ hPa, and added that to 900. The model is exponential, so the pressure falls by a constant factor per kilometer, not a constant amount.

items.stimulus: A paleobotanist compares fossil fern spores in a core sample with a reference layer. The paleobotanist models the change in relative abundance of the spores, in percentage points, as $f(x)$, where $x$ is the depth of a layer below the reference layer, in meters. According to the model, $f(0) = -20$ and $f(4) = -12$.
items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = a(x + 2)(x - b)$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. What is the value of $a + b$?
items.explanation: Substituting $x = 0$ gives $a(2)(-b) = -20$, so $ab = 10$. Substituting $x = 4$ gives $a(6)(4 - b) = -12$, so $a(4 - b) = -2$, which expands to $4a - ab = -2$. Replace $ab$ with 10: $4a - 10 = -2$, so $a = 2$. Then $b = 10 \div 2 = 5$, and $a + b = 7$.

B.why: 5 is the value of $b$ alone. You still need to add $a = 2$.

D.why: 10 is the product $ab$, which comes from the first substitution. You stopped before using the second point to separate $a$ from $b$.

items.stimulus: A nutrition scientist studies how vitamin C breaks down in bottled orange juice kept in the refrigerator. The scientist models the concentration of vitamin C as $f(t)$, in milligrams per liter, $t$ days after bottling. The juice has 200 milligrams per liter when it is bottled and 50 milligrams per liter 8 days later.
items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(t) = a \cdot b^{\frac{t}{4}}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: At bottling, $t = 0$, so $f(0) = a \cdot b^0 = a = 200$. At $t = 8$, the exponent is $\frac{8}{4} = 2$, so $200 \cdot b^2 = 50$. Then $b^2 = 0.25$, and because $b$ is positive, $b = 0.5$. The concentration halves every 4 days.

D.why: 200 is the value of $a$, the concentration at bottling, which you get by setting $t = 0$. The question asks for the base $b$.

items.stimulus: A nutrition scientist is working out how much seed coating each cracker in a test batch carries per unit of surface. Each cracker is a square with a side length of 6 centimeters.
items.stem: What is the area, in square centimeters, of one cracker?
items.explanation: The area of a square is $A = s^2$. With $s = 6$, $A = 6^2 = 36$ square centimeters.

C.why: You found the perimeter, $4 \times 6 = 24$ centimeters. The question asks for area, so you need $s^2$, not $4s$.

items.stimulus: A sports scientist uses a rectangular mat to test athletes' lateral jumps. The mat's length is 3 times its width, and its width is $w$ feet.
items.stem: Which expression represents the area, in square feet, of the mat?
items.explanation: The width is $w$ and the length is $3w$. Area is length times width: $A = (3w)(w) = 3w^2$ square feet.

D.why: You squared the length, $(3w)^2 = 9w^2$, as though the mat were a square with side $3w$. Multiply the length $3w$ by the width $w$ instead.

items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: In the shawl workshops of eighteenth-century Kashmir, a single design was divided among dozens of weavers, each responsible for one narrow strip that would later be stitched invisibly to its neighbors. A finished shawl might pass through a hundred hands. This ______ method of production, historians argue, explains how workshops could fill large orders while keeping each weaver's task simple.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The phrase "this ______ method" points back to the process just described: one design split into strips that separate weavers make and that are then joined. You need a word meaning "made one part at a time," and "piecemeal" means exactly that. It also fits the claim that the method kept each task simple.

A.why: "Desultory" means aimless or without a plan. The passage describes a carefully coordinated division of labor, so the word clashes with the process you just read about.

B.why: "Peripatetic" means traveling from place to place. It sounds like it could match a shawl passing "through a hundred hands," but the shawl moving between weavers is not the same as the method itself being itinerant. You picked a word that looks like the idea instead of one that means it.

D.why: "Cursory" means hasty and superficial. Strips stitched together "invisibly" show careful work, not rushed work. You may have reached for the familiar word because it seemed to fit roughly.

items.stimulus: Wheat farmers have long regarded clover growing between their rows as ______, a weed that robs the crop of water and soil nutrients. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The blank sits inside the old view that the trials then overturn. That view calls clover a weed that "robs" the crop, so the blank has to mean harmful. "Deleterious" means damaging, which is precisely that belief.

B.why: "Extraneous" means unnecessary or irrelevant. That fits the general idea of an unwanted weed, but the deciding word is "robs": farmers thought clover actively did damage, not just that it didn't matter. It is close in meaning but not precise.

items.stimulus: Mediterranean portolan charts of the fourteenth century were drawn for sailors, who needed accurate coastlines and compass bearings far more than information about what lay beyond the shore. D.why: "Ambivalently" means with mixed or conflicting feelings. It may sound like "vaguely" or "uncertainly," but the passage describes a clear choice about priorities, not divided feelings. You picked a word that resembles the idea you wanted.

items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: Fossil pollen resembling that of early magnolias has turned up in 95-million-year-old sediments from a single drill core in southern Patagonia. Some paleobotanists caution that the find offers only ______ evidence that flowering plants had reached the region by then: a lone sample could reflect contamination from younger layers, and no other core from the area has yet yielded similar grains.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The researchers "caution" and then say the sample "could" be contaminated. The evidence is weak but not ruled out. "Tenuous" means slight or flimsy, which is the right strength for a hedged warning.

A.why: "Incontrovertible" means impossible to dispute. The whole sentence is about how the evidence could be disputed.

B.why: "Tangential" means only loosely related. The pollen bears directly on the question; the worry is about how reliable it is, not whether it's relevant.

D.why: "Spurious" means false or not genuine. The researchers say only that contamination is possible ("could reflect"), not that the find is fake. You chose a word stronger than the hedged sentence supports.
