items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: Folklorist Nell Ashby calls the "stolen supper" tale strikingly ______. Among the versions she recorded from storytellers in eastern Kentucky, the trickster's name, the animal he outwits, and even whether he escapes unpunished all changed from one teller to the next; only the central ruse, in which he convinces his victim that the food is poisoned, stayed fixed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The next sentence defines the label: names, characters, and endings keep changing while one core element stays the same. "Protean" means able to take many forms, which fits a tale that shifts with every teller. Don't pass over it because it's less familiar.

A.why: "Apocryphal" means of doubtful authenticity. It fits the folklore topic, but Ashby says nothing about whether the tale is true or genuine, only that it varies. You matched the subject area instead of the logic.

B.why: "Immutable" means unchanging. Only the central ruse stays fixed, and the passage stresses how much else changes, so this reverses Ashby's point.

C.why: "Anachronistic" means out of its proper time period. Nothing in the passage is about chronology. The variation it describes is from teller to teller, not across eras.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Curators have long blamed the uneven fading of blue pigment in Edo-period woodblock prints on uneven exposure to light. Conservator Hana Ueda, however, found that in prints from the Kisaragi workshop, the blue near each sheet's edges is far more faded than the blue at the center, even in prints kept in dark storage and displayed only under uniform lighting. Workshop records show that its printers brushed a starch sizing onto each sheet from the center outward, leaving the edges thinly coated. Ueda therefore hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the Kisaragi printers applied less blue pigment near the edges of each sheet than at its center.
a heavier coating of starch sizing helps shield the blue pigment from whatever causes it to fade.
the edges of the Kisaragi prints received more light than their centers did while on display.
starch sizing speeds the fading of the blue pigment wherever it has been applied most heavily.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the edges faded more even though light was uniform, which rules out the curators' explanation. The one stated difference between edge and center is the sizing: thick at the center, where the blue survived, and thin at the edges, where it faded. The only explanation that fits every detail is that the sizing protects the pigment. Note that the choice does not say what causes the fading. It only says the sizing guards against it, which is as far as the passage goes.

A.why: The passage says nothing about how much pigment was applied, and 'faded' describes a change over time, not a lighter first coat. You replaced the sizing, the detail the passage actually gives you, with an explanation you invented.

C.why: This is the popular view that the passage sets up and then undercuts. The prints were kept in the dark and shown only under uniform lighting, so uneven light can't explain the pattern. You chose the belief the word 'however' tells you to reject.

D.why: This reverses the pattern. The heavy sizing is at the center, and the center is where the blue stayed strongest. If sizing sped up fading, the centers would be the most faded.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Folklorists often assume that a tale is best preserved near the place where it began. Yet the story of the Drowned Ferryman, which is set on the Varna River and is thought to have originated there, survives in mountain villages some 300 kilometers away but not in the villages along the river itself. Parish records show that the mountain villages were founded in the 1700s by families who fled the river valley after a series of floods, and that the valley was later resettled by migrants from the coast. These facts suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the tale began in the mountain villages and was later adapted to fit a setting on the Varna River.
the coastal migrants brought their own version of the tale with them when they resettled the valley.
tales are generally best preserved in places that lie far from where they first emerged.
the families who fled the floods carried the tale away with them, leaving no one in the valley to tell it.
items.explanation: The puzzle is that a river tale survives far from the river but not beside it. The records explain it. The valley's original people, who presumably told the tale, moved to the mountains, and the people who replaced them came from the coast. If the tale traveled with the displaced families, it would turn up in the mountains and be missing from the resettled valley, which is exactly what the passage describes.

A.why: This reverses where the tale came from. The tale is set on the Varna, and the mountain villages were founded by people from the valley, so every detail points to a valley origin. You explained the puzzle by ignoring the migration record.

B.why: The passage says the tale does not survive in the river villages, so the coastal migrants could not have planted a lasting version there. You overlooked the detail that the tale is missing from the valley.

C.why: One tale with an unusual history can't support a rule about tales in general. This choice flips the folklorists' generalization into an equally broad opposite one. The passage only explains this one case.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: At most Bronze Age settlements in the Harrow Basin, the proportion of sheep bones to cattle bones rises during droughts, since sheep need far less water and forage than cattle do. At the settlement of Tell Omran, however, pollen records show a severe drought around 1900 BCE, yet cattle bones from that period outnumber those from wetter centuries. Sediment cores reveal that a spring-fed marsh beside Tell Omran stayed wet throughout the drought. The researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the marsh let Tell Omran keep cattle at a time when drought made them hard to keep elsewhere.
the drought around 1900 BCE was far less severe in the basin than the pollen records indicate.
sheep in the Harrow Basin needed more water and forage than researchers have usually assumed.
Tell Omran's residents hunted wild cattle more often than residents of other settlements did.
items.explanation: Normally drought shifts herds toward sheep, because cattle need more water and forage. Tell Omran went the other way. The one thing that sets it apart is a marsh that stayed wet through the drought. A reliable source of water and grazing explains why cattle could still be kept there, and even thrive, while the rest of the basin lost them.

B.why: The passage states that the pollen records show a severe drought. Doubting that evidence ignores the detail that makes Tell Omran unusual, the marsh that stayed wet. This is the trap of an explanation that sounds scientific but skips the setting.

C.why: The passage states that sheep need far less water and forage than cattle, and that the sheep-heavy pattern holds at most sites. This choice goes against that premise and still doesn't explain why Tell Omran differs.

D.why: Nothing in the passage mentions hunting or wild animals. You invented a new factor and ignored the marsh, which is the one local difference the passage points out.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In most corn-growing regions, planting a winter rye cover crop raises the yield of the corn that follows, largely because rye residue holds moisture in the soil through early summer. Agronomists studying the Lowmoor district, where spring rains are unusually heavy, expected this benefit to reverse there: the extra moisture held by rye residue, they reasoned, would keep already saturated fields waterlogged and force farmers to delay planting. They therefore anticipated that in Lowmoor, corn planted after rye would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: yield more than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
grow in soil that dried out faster than the soil of Lowmoor fields left bare over winter.
yield less than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
yield less than corn planted without rye in every region, regardless of spring rainfall.
items.explanation: The passage tells you the usual benefit will reverse in Lowmoor. Usually, corn after rye yields more than corn without rye. Flipped, corn after rye in Lowmoor yields less than corn without rye in Lowmoor. The reasoning given (waterlogged fields and delayed planting) supports a lower yield, and the comparison stays within Lowmoor.

A.why: This is the usual effect, not the reversed one. The agronomists expected the benefit to reverse in Lowmoor, and you kept the original direction.

B.why: The agronomists' reasoning is that rye residue holds extra moisture, so soil after rye should stay wetter, not dry out faster. This choice reverses the mechanism the passage relies on.

D.why: The reversal is predicted only for Lowmoor, because of its heavy spring rains. The passage says rye raises yields in most regions, so 'every region, regardless of spring rainfall' goes far beyond what was expected. Watch for words like 'every' and 'regardless.'

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Inspectors of the Carrow Viaduct found that the steel expansion joints at its north end had rusted through in half the time expected, while identical joints at the south end, installed the same year and carrying the same traffic, showed little rust. The viaduct's north end sits in the shadow of a cliff for most of the day, so snow and slush treated with deicing salt linger there for days after storms, whereas the sunlit south end clears within hours. The inspectors hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the cold at the shaded north end made its steel joints brittle and prone to cracking.
prolonged contact with salty meltwater caused the north joints to corrode more quickly.
the north joints were made from a lower grade of steel than the joints at the south end.
direct sunlight at the south end slowly damaged its joints as well, though less visibly.
items.explanation: The joints are identical, were installed the same year and carry the same traffic, so none of those explains the difference. What differs is how long salty slush sits on each end: days on the north, hours on the south. The damage is rust, and longer contact with salt water is a direct cause of rust. This explanation fits both the setting and the kind of damage.

A.why: This fixes on the shade and the cold but misses what the shade does in the passage, which is keep salty slush in place. It also describes brittleness and cracking, while the damage the inspectors found was rust. The explanation sounds scientific but doesn't match the damage.

C.why: The passage calls the joints identical. You explained the difference with a variable the passage has already ruled out.

D.why: The passage gives no sign that sunlight harms steel, and the south joints are described as showing little rust. This choice invents hidden damage instead of explaining why the north end rusted.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: A team testing a new self-healing polymer found that cracks near the surface of a sample sealed within a day, while cracks deep inside the same sample were still open a week later. The healing agent had been distributed evenly throughout the polymer, and all samples were kept at a constant temperature. Because the agent is known to react with water, and the surface is the only part of the material in contact with humid air, the team hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the interior cracks were larger than the surface cracks and so required more healing agent.
the healing agent had settled toward the surface of the sample before the polymer hardened.
water vapor in the air slows the healing reaction, so cracks near the surface should close last.
moisture from the surrounding air drives the healing reaction that seals the surface cracks.
items.explanation: Two possible causes are ruled out: the agent was spread evenly, and the temperature was held constant. The one remaining difference between surface and interior is contact with humid air, and the agent is known to react with water. If moisture from the air drives the reaction, surface cracks should heal quickly and deep cracks slowly, which is what the team saw.

A.why: The passage gives no information about crack size. You made up a difference and skipped the one the passage points to: water and humid air.

B.why: The passage says the healing agent was distributed evenly throughout the polymer. This choice depends on the agent being concentrated at the surface, which the setup rules out.

C.why: This gets the effect backward. The surface cracks, the only ones exposed to humid air, sealed fastest. A hypothesis that has them closing last contradicts the result it's supposed to explain.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Thick leaf cuticles, waxy coatings that limit water loss, are usually read as a sign that a plant grew in a dry climate. Fossils of the extinct shrub Salicornites, however, have unusually thick cuticles yet were found rooted in growth position in coastal swamp deposits. Other plants preserved in the same deposits, which grew farther from the shoreline, have thin cuticles, and chemical analysis shows that the water around Salicornites was highly salty. Plant roots struggle to draw water from salty soil. Paleobotanists therefore hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the regional climate was dry when Salicornites lived, even though the shrub grew in a swamp.
Salicornites leaves were carried into the swamp from drier upland areas after they had fallen.
thick cuticles helped Salicornites hold on to water that its roots could take up only poorly.
all plants that grew in salty coastal swamps developed thick cuticles like those of Salicornites.
items.explanation: The key detail is the comparison group. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, so the climate as a whole wasn't dry. What set Salicornites apart was salty water, and the passage says roots struggle to draw water from salty soil. A plant that can't take up water easily would benefit from losing less of it, which explains the thick cuticles without needing a dry climate.

A.why: This is the usual reading that the passage undercuts. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, which wouldn't fit a dry regional climate. You applied the rule of thumb and ignored the comparison group.

B.why: The fossils were found rooted in growth position, so Salicornites grew where it was preserved. It wasn't washed in from somewhere else.

D.why: The passage describes one shrub in one swamp. Stretching that to 'all plants' in every salty swamp is strength creep that the evidence can't support.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Roads usually lower the nesting success of forest songbirds, because the open edges they create draw nest predators such as crows. In the Elden Forest, however, wood thrush nests within 100 meters of a road fledge young more often than nests deeper in the forest. The forest's chief nest predator is not a crow but the eastern ratsnake, which basks on warm pavement and is frequently killed by vehicles. The researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: traffic keeps ratsnake numbers low near roads, leaving thrush nests there less exposed.
road edges in the Elden Forest draw ratsnakes, which then raid the thrush nests nearby.
thrushes nesting near roads find more insects for their young than thrushes elsewhere do.
roads raise the nesting success of every songbird species that breeds in the Elden Forest.
items.explanation: The surprise is that nests near roads do better, which is the opposite of the usual pattern. The passage explains why: the main predator here is a snake that basks on pavement and is often killed by cars. If traffic thins out the snakes near roads, fewer predators reach the nearby nests, and those nests fledge more young.

B.why: This is the usual pattern, roads drawing predators to nests, applied where the passage says it reverses. If roads drew raiding snakes, nests near roads would do worse, but they do better. You also skipped the detail that the snakes are frequently killed by vehicles.

C.why: The passage never mentions food. It builds its explanation around the predator. A made-up factor that ignores the ratsnake doesn't use the details you were given.

D.why: The finding is about wood thrush nests only. 'Every songbird species' stretches one species' result to a whole community, which is strength creep the passage can't support.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Obsidian blades are abundant at Ravna Kosa, a hilltop settlement occupied around 3000 BCE, yet the nearest obsidian source is a volcanic field some 300 kilometers away. Producing a blade from a raw obsidian core generates hundreds of small flakes and chips, debris that typically accumulates wherever the knapping takes place. Archaeologist Mira Sotelo hypothesizes that the settlement's residents did not make the blades themselves but instead received them as finished tools.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sotelo's hypothesis?
choices: Chemical analysis shows that the blades' obsidian matches the composition of rock from the volcanic field 300 kilometers away.
Excavations across the settlement have recovered very few of the small obsidian flakes and chips produced during blade making.
Microscopic wear on the blades' edges indicates that most of them were used to cut plant fibers rather than meat.
Several large, partially worked obsidian cores have been recovered from the floors of houses at the settlement.
items.explanation: The claim's key term is 'finished tools': the blades were not made at Ravna Kosa. The passage tells you that making blades leaves heaps of flakes wherever the work happens. If almost no such debris turns up at the site, the knapping probably happened somewhere else, so the blades arrived already made. That makes the claim more likely.

A.why: You picked a true-sounding, on-topic fact that doesn't touch the claim. The passage already says the obsidian came from far away. What's in question is whether it arrived as finished blades or as raw cores, and a chemical match can't tell those apart.

C.why: You picked a detail about how the blades were used. The claim is about where they were made, and edge wear says nothing about that.

D.why: Partly worked cores inside houses would mean residents were making blades themselves, which weakens Sotelo's hypothesis rather than supporting it.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Many coral larvae settle preferentially on crustose coralline algae, a pink alga that coats reef rock. The algae offer both a distinctive rough surface and chemical compounds released by living cells. To separate these factors, a team placed larvae in two tanks. One held tiles coated with live algae; the other held tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached, which kept the same rough surface but released no compounds. The team hypothesized that chemical cues, not surface texture, drive the larvae's preference.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
choices: Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on smooth tiles that had no algae at all.
Larvae that settled on tiles coated with live algae grew faster during their first month than larvae on other surfaces.
Larvae settled at similar rates on tiles coated with live algae and on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
items.explanation: The two tanks match on texture and differ only in chemical cues. If the hypothesis is right, larvae should strongly prefer the live-algae tiles over the dead-algae tiles, even though both surfaces are equally rough. That is exactly what this choice reports.

A.why: You picked a result that supports a broader idea: larvae prefer algae. Smooth bare tiles differ from live-algae tiles in both texture and chemistry, so this result can't show which factor matters, and that is the whole claim.

B.why: You picked a fact about growth after settling. The hypothesis is about what makes larvae choose where to settle.

C.why: If larvae settled equally on both tiles, removing the chemical cues changed nothing. That points to texture and weakens the hypothesis.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Some self-healing plastics contain tiny capsules of liquid healing agent scattered among particles of a catalyst. When a crack forms, it ruptures nearby capsules; the released liquid flows into the crack, where contact with the catalyst makes it harden and bond the crack shut. Samples tested at -20°C recover far less of their original strength than samples tested at room temperature. Materials scientist Priya Anand argues that the cold does not prevent the capsules from breaking but instead slows the hardening reaction.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Anand's claim?
choices: In cracked cold samples, the capsules along the crack were broken and empty, but the liquid inside the crack had not hardened.
Cracked cold samples recovered less than a third of their original strength, while room-temperature samples recovered nearly all of it.
In cracked cold samples, most of the capsules along the crack were still intact and full of liquid healing agent.
At room temperature, samples containing more capsules recovered more strength than samples containing fewer capsules.
items.explanation: Anand's claim has two parts: the capsules still break in the cold, and the failure happens later, at the hardening step. Empty capsules show the liquid was released. Unhardened liquid in the crack shows the reaction is where the process stalled. Both parts are confirmed.

B.why: You picked a choice that just repeats, with numbers, the weaker recovery the passage already describes. Anand is explaining why that happens, and this choice doesn't say which step failed.

C.why: Intact capsules would mean the cold stopped them from breaking. That is the very explanation Anand rejects.

D.why: You picked a fact about how many capsules there are, and only at room temperature. It says nothing about what the cold does to the process.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: In many cities, songbirds sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in the countryside, a shift that may help their songs carry over low-frequency traffic noise. The difference could arise because urban populations have gradually developed fixed, higher-pitched songs over many generations. Ornithologist Tomás Irigoyen, however, contends that individual birds adjust their pitch flexibly, raising it only when the surrounding noise is loud.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Irigoyen's claim?
choices: Across twelve cities, songbirds' average pitch was higher in cities with heavy traffic than in cities with light traffic.
Songbirds living in cities were found to begin singing earlier each morning than songbirds living in the countryside.
The same individual birds sang at a higher pitch during weekday rush hours than during quiet weekend mornings.
Chicks of urban birds raised in quiet aviaries developed the same high-pitched songs as their parents.
items.explanation: The key terms are 'individual' and 'flexibly'. Irigoyen says one bird changes its pitch as the noise changes. If the same birds sing higher when traffic is loud and lower when it's quiet, that is flexible adjustment within each bird.

A.why: You picked a result that links noise and pitch, which is broader than the claim. A comparison between cities fits fixed, inherited songs just as well as flexible ones, so it can't settle the question Irigoyen is answering.

B.why: You picked a fact about when birds sing. The claim is about pitch and noise.

D.why: Chicks that develop high songs even without noise suggest the pitch is fixed and inherited. That is the alternative Irigoyen argues against.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Anders Holt's 1672 chart of the northern Baltic coast was prized by navigators for its detailed depiction of harbors and inlets, though its interior regions are sketchy and often misplaced. Holt left no account of how he gathered his information. After studying the chart, historian Lena Marsh concluded that Holt drew the coastline not from surveys of his own but by compiling the written logs kept by ship pilots.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marsh's conclusion?
choices: Holt's chart depicts the region's harbors and inlets far more accurately than any earlier chart of the region does.
Harbor names on Holt's chart repeat unusual misspellings found in surviving pilots' logs from the same decade.
Holt's chart was copied by several later mapmakers, some of whom still relied on it as late as the 1720s.
Holt's account books record wages he paid to a survey crew during the years he worked on the chart.
items.explanation: Marsh's conclusion names a specific source: pilots' written logs. If the chart repeats the logs' own odd spellings, Holt was very likely copying from those documents. That points straight at the source she identifies.

A.why: You picked an accurate, on-topic fact about how good the chart is. Accurate coastlines could come from Holt's own surveys or from pilots' logs, so this doesn't show where his information came from.

C.why: You picked a fact about the chart's later influence. The claim is about how Holt gathered his information in the first place.

D.why: Paying a survey crew suggests Holt did his own surveying, which is what Marsh concluded he did not do.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Over the past decade, a new pronunciation of the vowel in words such as "fell" has spread among teenagers in the city of Harlow Bay, having first appeared in a single eastern neighborhood. Some researchers attribute the spread to popular online videos featuring speakers from that neighborhood. Linguist Dana Okafor, however, argues that the pronunciation has spread chiefly through teenagers' face-to-face friendships rather than through media exposure.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's argument?
choices: Teenagers with close friends from the eastern neighborhood adopted the pronunciation early, whether or not they watched the videos.
Teenagers throughout the city use the new pronunciation far more often than their parents and grandparents do.
Teenagers who watched the videos adopted the pronunciation early, even if they had no friends from the eastern neighborhood.
A similar vowel change spread through a neighboring city about fifty years before it appeared in Harlow Bay.
items.explanation: Okafor's claim sets friendships against media. This finding separates the two: having friends from the neighborhood predicts early adoption, and watching the videos doesn't. That is the pattern her argument predicts.

B.why: You picked a choice that confirms teenagers are driving the change, which the passage already assumes. It says nothing about whether friendships or media spread it.

C.why: If watching the videos is enough without any friendships, that supports the media explanation Okafor rejects.

D.why: You picked a historical parallel in another city. It doesn't tell you how the pronunciation is spreading in Harlow Bay.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Mice raised in sterile conditions, without gut bacteria, respond weakly to certain vaccines, suggesting that gut microbes help the immune system develop. To test when such exposure matters, researchers gave one group of these germ-free mice gut bacteria shortly after birth and gave an otherwise identical group the same bacteria as adults, then vaccinated both groups. The researchers hypothesized that microbial exposure strengthens vaccine responses only if it occurs early in life.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Germ-free mice that never received gut bacteria responded to the vaccine more weakly than mice raised in ordinary conditions.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth gained weight faster in their first month than mice that stayed germ-free.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth and mice given bacteria as adults responded to the vaccine equally strongly.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth responded strongly to the vaccine, but mice given bacteria as adults responded weakly.
items.explanation: The deciding words are 'only if' and 'early in life'. The hypothesis predicts a gap between the groups: exposure right after birth helps, and exposure in adulthood doesn't. A strong response in the newborn group and a weak one in the adult group is that gap.

A.why: You picked a choice that supports the broader idea that microbes matter, which the passage already states. It says nothing about timing, and timing is the entire hypothesis.

B.why: You picked a fact about weight gain. The hypothesis is about vaccine responses.

C.why: Equal responses would mean the timing of exposure makes no difference, which weakens the 'only if early' hypothesis.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Summer thunderstorms occur more often downwind of some large cities than upwind of them. One explanation holds that pavement and buildings heat the air above the city, which rises and forms storm clouds. Another holds that airborne particles from traffic and industry give water vapor surfaces on which to condense, seeding clouds. Meteorologist Ivan Petrov maintains that the city's heat, not its particle pollution, is the main trigger of the extra storms.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Petrov's claim?
choices: Most of the airborne particles over the city come from vehicle traffic rather than from factories and power plants.
Summer thunderstorms occur roughly 25 percent more often in areas downwind of the city than in areas upwind of it.
On days when airborne particle levels were unusually low, the downwind increase in storms was as large as on typical days.
On unusually cool summer days, the downwind increase in storms was as large as on the hottest days of the season.
items.explanation: Petrov compares two causes and ranks heat above particles. If storms stay just as frequent when particles are scarce, particles can't be the main trigger. That leaves heat as the better explanation.

A.why: You picked a fact about where the particles come from. Both traffic and industry fall under the particle explanation, so this doesn't separate it from the heat explanation.

B.why: You picked a choice that just puts a number on the pattern both explanations are trying to account for. It doesn't favor heat over particles.

D.why: If the extra storms continue even when the city is cool, heat is not the trigger. That weakens Petrov's claim.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Public health researchers tested a program that sent text-message reminders about flu vaccination to adults in one county. Before the program began, each participant completed a survey stating whether they intended to be vaccinated that season. Vaccination rates among participants rose after the reminders were sent. The researchers claim that the reminders worked mainly by prompting people who already intended to be vaccinated to follow through, not by persuading people who had not planned to be vaccinated.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' claim?
choices: Participants who received the reminders were vaccinated at a higher rate than similar adults in the county who received no reminders.
Among participants who had planned to be vaccinated, rates rose sharply, while among those who had not, rates barely changed.
Participants who had not planned to be vaccinated became much more likely to be vaccinated after receiving the reminders.
Most participants reported in a follow-up survey that the reminder messages had been clear and easy to understand.
items.explanation: The claim is about *who* the reminders affected: people who already intended to get vaccinated, not people who didn't. For support, the rise has to show up among intenders and be missing among non-intenders. Choice B shows exactly that split, so if it's true you would believe the claim more.

A.why: You picked a finding that shows the reminders worked at all. The claim goes further and says how they worked, and this choice doesn't separate intenders from non-intenders, so it supports a broader idea than the one claimed.

C.why: You matched the topic but missed the direction. If non-intenders were persuaded, the reminders did change minds, which is the very thing the researchers say did not happen.

D.why: You chose an on-topic fact about the messages. Whether they were clear says nothing about which group of participants they moved.

items.stimulus: Sediment cores show that a river near a Bronze Age settlement in the Carpathian Basin shifted its course around 1400 BCE, the same period in which the settlement was abandoned. Archaeologist Réka Hollós argues that the shift drove residents away not by flooding their homes but by raising the local water table, which spoiled the grain they stored in pits dug beneath their house floors.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hollós's claim?
choices: The house floors are covered by a thick layer of silt of the kind a river leaves behind after it floods.
Several other settlements along the same river were also abandoned at some point around 1400 BCE.
Residents of the settlement grew both barley and wheat, which were the main crops throughout the region.
The storage pits contain grain showing signs of water damage, while the floors above show no flood deposits.
items.explanation: Hollós's claim is a chain: the river shifted, the water table rose, the stored grain spoiled, and the residents left. She also rules out flooding. Choice D supports the middle link (water-damaged grain in the pits) and the exclusion (no flood deposits on the floors), so it backs her specific explanation.

C.why: You picked an accurate-sounding fact about the settlement's grain. Which crops the residents grew doesn't show whether rising groundwater spoiled them.

The impressions share identical outlines and details, showing that they were all printed from one block.
The woodcut's harbor scene closely resembles harbor scenes painted by artists working in the same city.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: During the 1700s, weavers in one district of northern England largely abandoned wool in favor of linen. Linen required different spinning skills, but it could be woven on the same looms. Historian Thomas Ashdown claims that the change was driven by a shortage of local wool caused by disease among the district's sheep, not by a shift in what buyers wanted.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ashdown's claim?
choices: Weavers in the district were able to weave linen on the same looms they had previously used for wool.
Buyers throughout England increasingly preferred linen garments to woolen ones during the 1700s.
The district's sheep numbers fell by half just before the change, while local demand for wool held steady.
Disease reduced sheep populations in many parts of Europe during the century before the change.
items.explanation: Ashdown's claim has two parts: a local wool shortage caused the switch, and buyer demand did not. Choice C supports both. The district's flocks shrank right before the change, and demand for wool stayed the same, which rules out a shift in taste.

A.why: You repeated a detail from the passage. Being able to reuse the looms made the switch easier, but it doesn't show that a wool shortage caused it.

B.why: You supported the rival explanation. A change in buyer preference is exactly what Ashdown says was not the cause.

D.why: You chose a broader, earlier fact. Disease elsewhere in Europe a century before doesn't show that this district's sheep declined when its weavers switched.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Astronomers have recorded repeated episodes in which a distant star dims for several weeks. Dust lying between a star and observers blocks blue light more strongly than infrared light, whereas a drop in a star's own energy output dims all wavelengths by roughly the same amount. A team studying the star concluded that its dimming is caused by an orbiting dust cloud passing in front of it rather than by changes in the star itself.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
choices: During the most recent episode, the star's total brightness dropped by roughly 20 percent.
During each episode, the star dimmed about three times as much in blue light as in infrared.
During each episode, the star dimmed by about the same amount in blue light as in infrared.
Several other stars in the same region of the sky have also been observed dimming for weeks.
items.explanation: The passage tells you how to test the claim: dust dims blue light more than infrared, and changes in the star itself dim both equally. Uneven dimming, stronger in blue, points to dust, so Choice B supports the team's conclusion.

A.why: You chose a fact about how much the star dimmed. The size of the drop doesn't separate dust from a change in the star, because only the difference between wavelengths does that.

C.why: You reversed the test. According to the passage, equal dimming at both wavelengths points to a change in the star itself, which is the explanation the team rejects.

D.why: You were drawn by topic overlap. Other stars dimming says nothing about what causes this star to dim.

items.stimulus: Curb extensions widen the sidewalk at a street corner, shortening the distance pedestrians must walk to cross. After a city added curb extensions at forty intersections, its planners reviewed five years of injury reports. The planners claim that curb extensions reduce pedestrian injuries at intersections with heavy traffic, even if they do little at quiet intersections.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the planners' claim?
choices: At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell 40 percent after extensions were added but held steady at similar ones without them.
Across all of the city's intersections, pedestrian injuries fell by about 8 percent during the five years reviewed.
At quiet intersections, pedestrian injury counts were about the same before and after curb extensions were added.
At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell by similar amounts whether or not curb extensions had been added.
items.explanation: The scope words are 'at intersections with heavy traffic.' To support the claim, a finding has to show a drop at busy intersections that can be credited to the extensions. Choice A shows a large drop where extensions were added and none at comparable intersections without them.

D.why: You overlooked the comparison. If injuries fell just as much without extensions, something other than the extensions caused the drop, which undercuts the claim.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of 2 in this context?

The frequency increases by 440 hertz for every 12 semitones above A4.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A printmaking studio has two etching presses. Working alone, the older press finishes a run of posters in $a$ hours and the newer press finishes the same run in $b$ hours. Working together, they finish the run in $T$ hours, where $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $T$ and $b$?
items.explanation: First isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. Over the common denominator $Tb$ this is $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{b - T}{Tb}$. Then take reciprocals of both sides to get $a = \frac{Tb}{b - T}$. As a check, with $T = 2$ and $b = 3$ the original equation gives $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $a = 6$, and $\frac{2 \cdot 3}{3 - 2} = 6$.

A.why: You flipped each fraction separately, turning $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ into $T = a + b$. You can't undo a sum of reciprocals one term at a time.

B.why: This is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $a$. You combined the fractions correctly but skipped the last step of taking the reciprocal.

D.why: You reversed the subtraction when combining $\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. The numerator should be $b - T$. Your version gives a negative time, because two presses together finish faster than either press alone, so $T < b$.

items.stimulus: A linguist compares a bilingual corpus in which $w$ sentences are in Welsh and $n$ sentences are in English, where $w > n$. The linguist measures the corpus's imbalance with the index $R = \frac{w - n}{w + n}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $R$, $w$, and $n$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $R$ and $n$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $w + n$ to get $Rw + Rn = w - n$. Collect the $w$ terms on one side: $Rn + n = w - Rw$. Factor both sides: $n(1 + R) = w(1 - R)$. Divide by $1 - R$: $w = \frac{n(1 + R)}{1 - R}$. As a check, with $n = 1$ and $R = \frac{1}{2}$ this gives $w = 3$, and $\frac{3 - 1}{3 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$.

A.why: You mixed up the signs when collecting terms, so the numerator and denominator traded places. Test $n = 1$ and $R = \frac{1}{2}$: this choice gives $w = \frac{1}{3}$, which is smaller than $n$.

B.why: You moved $Rw$ but then treated $w - Rw$ as just $w$. Because $w$ appears in two terms, you have to factor it out as $w(1 - R)$ and divide by $1 - R$.

C.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $Rw$ across. Since $R < 1$, the denominator $R - 1$ is negative, so this choice makes $w$ negative, which breaks the condition that $w$ is positive.

per_choice.B: You moved $Rw$ but then treated $w - Rw$ as just $w$. Because $w$ appears in two terms, you have to factor it out as $w(1 - R)$ and divide by $1 - R$.
per_choice.C: You dropped a sign when you moved $Rw$ across. Since $R < 1$, the denominator $R - 1$ is negative, so this choice makes $w$ negative, which breaks the condition that $w$ is positive.

items.stimulus: An agricultural scientist blends $x$ kilograms of fertilizer that is $a$ percent nitrogen with $y$ kilograms of fertilizer that is $b$ percent nitrogen, where $b < a$. The blend is $C$ percent nitrogen, where $b < C < a$ and $C = \frac{ax + by}{x + y}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $C$, $a$, $b$, $x$, and $y$. Which equation correctly expresses $x$ in terms of $C$, $a$, $b$, and $y$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $x + y$ to get $Cx + Cy = ax + by$. Collect the $x$ terms on one side: $Cy - by = ax - Cx$. Factor both sides: $y(C - b) = x(a - C)$. items.stimulus: A folklorist builds a spread index $d$ for a trickster tale. It combines $p$, the number of villages where the tale was recorded in spoken form, and $q$, the number of villages where it appears in written collections, using $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q}$.

items.explanation: Combine the right side over the common denominator $pq$: $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{p + q}{pq}$. Take reciprocals to get $d^2 = \frac{pq}{p + q}$. Because $d$ is positive, keep the positive root: $d = \sqrt{\frac{pq}{p + q}}$.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Wage Ledger is a 1911 novel by Marguerite Osler. Its central figure, Hollis Crane, is a clerk at a shipyard where the owners have just lowered the piece rates paid to riveters. Crane's job is to calculate and record each man's earnings under the new rates. In a study of the novel, one scholar argues that Crane privately doubts the fairness of the reduced rates even as he applies them with scrupulous care:
items.stem: Which quotation from The Wage Ledger most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "He entered each reduced rate in his neatest hand, pausing only to wonder whether the men who earned it could live on it."
"Crane had never once miscounted a riveter's wage, and the owners trusted his ledger far above their own accounts."
"The new rates struck him as a cruelty, and at night he lay awake composing protests he knew he would never send."
"Crane refused to enter the new rates, telling the foreman that no honest clerk could put his name to such figures."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Crane doubts that the lower rates are fair, and he still applies them carefully. items.stimulus: Grid and Garden, a 1924 novel by Philip Stane, follows Lydia Marsh, an engineer hired to redesign a crowded industrial town. The book is often assigned in urban planning courses for its portrait of early zoning debates. One planning historian argues that Marsh favours straight, efficient streets only in the commercial district, and that she insists the residential quarters keep their old winding lanes:

"She drew every avenue straight across the map, from the warehouses right out to the farthest row of cottages."
"Marsh loved the old town's twisting alleys, where she had wandered as a child among the bakers and the bookbinders."
"The council argued for a full week over the cost of paving the broad new streets of the commercial quarter."

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Harlan Vosk's 1931 play The Tally Room is set in a fish cannery where workers are paid according to the total number of cans their whole line produces, not by individual output. Under this system, one slow worker lowers everyone's pay. Labour economists sometimes use the play to illustrate group incentives. One economist claims that Nell Garrity, the play's central figure, grasps this link and presses slower coworkers to keep pace because of it:
items.stem: Which quotation from The Tally Room most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Hurry yourself along, Tom, or the whole lot of us will be stuck here long past the evening whistle again."
"The bosses count the cans at the end of the line, and they pay the whole line together, not the single girl."
"I'll work at whatever pace suits me, Tom; my wage is my own affair and nobody else's business at all."
"Pick it up, Tom. Every can you miss on this line comes out of my pay envelope as well as out of yours."
items.explanation: The claim has a chain: Nell understands that pay is shared across the line, and that is why she pushes coworkers. Here she tells Tom to speed up, and her reason is that every can he misses lowers her pay as well as his. The line shows both the pressure and the pay link behind it.

B.why: This line explains how pay is shared across the line, but Nell never presses anyone to work faster. It gives the mechanism without the action, so it is only half the claim.

C.why: Here Nell calls her wage her own affair. That denies the very link between her pay and her coworkers' output that the claim says she understands.

items.stimulus: In Ottilie Farrant's 1896 novel The Blank Margin, the mapmaker Jonas Pell is commissioned to chart a northern province, much of which no surveyor has yet visited. "The duke admired maps crowded with sea monsters and would pay handsomely for an elaborately painted border."

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Seismologists have generally regarded slow slip events, in which a fault creeps for weeks without producing noticeable shaking, as a kind of safety valve: by releasing built-up stress gradually, they were thought to lower the odds of a large earthquake. However, seismologist Mereana Tuhi's analysis of the Hikurangi margin off New Zealand found that several slow slip events shifted stress onto neighboring locked sections of the fault, where swarms of small earthquakes followed. Tuhi notes that her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, but she argues that slow slip should no longer be viewed simply as a release of danger.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Swarms of small earthquakes occurred on locked sections of the Hikurangi margin after several slow slip events.
Slow slip events release stress so gradually that small earthquakes seldom follow them along the Hikurangi margin.
Evidence that slow slip events can shift stress to nearby fault sections challenges the view that they simply reduce earthquake risk.
Tuhi's analysis demonstrates that slow slip events make major earthquakes more likely on neighboring fault sections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the accepted view that slow slip is a safety valve. After 'However,' it brings in Tuhi's finding that slow slip can move stress onto neighboring sections, and it ends with her argument that the old view is too simple. Choice C covers the expected view, the finding and the conclusion without claiming more than Tuhi does.

A.why: You picked a detail that is accurate but only one step in the argument. The swarms are evidence. The passage uses them to challenge an assumption, and this choice leaves that challenge out.

B.why: You probably recognised 'release stress' from the opening and stopped reading. The passage says swarms of small earthquakes did follow slow slip, which is the opposite of 'seldom follow.'

D.why: You missed the hedge. Tuhi explicitly says her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, so 'demonstrates' claims something she refuses to claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves record not only which plants once grew in a place but also the climate they grew in. Among living woody plants, species with smooth leaf edges are more common in warm regions, while toothed edges predominate in cool ones. For example, when paleobotanist Ines Varga examined a 52-million-year-old leaf bed in the Dunmore Formation, she found that only about a fifth of its species had toothed edges, pointing to a warm climate. That estimate closely matched temperatures inferred independently from chemical signatures in nearby marine sediments.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Only about a fifth of the species in the Dunmore Formation leaf bed had leaves with toothed edges.
The shapes of fossil leaves can provide evidence about ancient climates, as Varga's study of one leaf bed illustrates.
Leaf shape gives more accurate estimates of ancient temperatures than chemical signatures in marine sediments do.
Fossil leaf beds reveal much about which plants once grew in a place but little about the climates of the past.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes the general claim that fossil leaves record climate. Everything after 'For example' is one case that supports it. Choice B states the general claim and ties Varga's study to it, so it covers the whole passage.

A.why: You chose a statistic from the example. It is correct, but it is there only to support the opening claim about what fossil leaves can reveal.

C.why: You read a ranking into the passage. The two estimates 'closely matched,' and the text never says leaf shape is more accurate than the sediment chemistry.

D.why: The first half of this choice matches the opening, but the second half reverses it. The passage's point is that fossil leaves reveal climate as well as plants.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds to every threat as if meeting it for the first time. Recent studies suggest this division may be too tidy. After people receive certain vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis, their monocytes, a type of innate immune cell, can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months. The effect appears briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, but it suggests the innate branch may be capable of a limited kind of memory.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After BCG vaccination, monocytes can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months.
Innate immune cells appear to remember specific pathogens as durably and precisely as adaptive cells do.
Vaccines such as BCG can protect people against nearly any microbe by strengthening their innate immune cells.
The innate immune branch, long thought to lack memory, may possess a limited and less targeted form of it.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the traditional split, says it 'may be too tidy,' gives the BCG evidence, and ends with a hedged conclusion that innate cells may have a limited memory. Choice D keeps both the claim and its limits: 'may' and 'limited and less targeted.'

A.why: You chose the evidence instead of what it shows. The monocyte finding is accurate, but the passage uses it to question how immunologists divide the immune system.

B.why: You kept 'innate cells remember' and dropped the qualification. The passage says the effect is briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, not equally durable and precise.

C.why: You stretched the finding into a big claim about protection. The text reports stronger responses to some unrelated microbes for months. It never says people are protected against nearly any microbe.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Print collectors have long prized the earliest impressions from a run, assuming that later ones show a block worn down by repeated pressing. The linocuts of Hedda Lorne, a printmaker active in the 1920s, complicate that assumption. Lorne regularly recut her blocks between printings, adding figures and deepening shadows, and she adjusted her inks from one batch to the next. In letters, she called her late impressions 'the finished picture.' For Lorne's work, then, a later impression may be not a degraded copy but the version she most intended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: For Lorne's linocuts, later impressions may represent the artist's intended work rather than inferior copies.
Lorne adjusted the inks she used for her linocuts from one batch of impressions to the next.
Later impressions of prints are generally more valuable than early ones, as Lorne's letters demonstrate.
Lorne's linocuts confirm that early impressions preserve details that are lost as a block wears down.

D.why: This repeats the collectors' assumption that the passage says Lorne's work complicates. Her prints challenge that view instead of confirming it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Dietary guidelines usually treat fiber as a single nutrient, recommending a daily total in grams. However, research led by nutrition scientist Priya Anand suggests that total may be only part of the story. Different fibers feed different gut bacteria, and in Anand's trial, an inulin supplement sharply raised levels of beneficial Bifidobacterium in most participants but barely changed them in others, depending on which microbes each person already carried. Anand concludes that fiber's effects likely depend on both the kind of fiber and the eater's existing gut community.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In Anand's trial, an inulin supplement raised levels of Bifidobacterium in most of the participants.
Fiber supplements do not benefit people whose gut bacteria differ from those of most other people.
Fiber's effects may depend on the type of fiber and a person's gut microbes, not only on the total eaten.
Anand's research confirms that all types of fiber affect the gut's bacteria in much the same way.
items.explanation: After 'However,' the passage argues that a daily total is only part of the story, and Anand's conclusion names the two factors that also matter. Choice C gives both factors, contrasts them with the single-total view, and keeps the hedge.

D.why: The passage says different fibers feed different bacteria. That is the opposite of claiming all fibers act in much the same way.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the decade after beavers were reintroduced to a river in the Scottish Borders, surveys recorded a marked rise in the number of dragonfly species along its banks. Ecologist Callum Reid considers it plausible that the beavers were responsible, since their dams create the still, plant-rich ponds in which many dragonfly larvae thrive. But the same decade also brought new limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms, which may have improved water quality. Establishing the beavers' role, Reid argues, will require comparing this river with similar ones where beavers are absent.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The reintroduction of beavers caused the number of dragonfly species along the river to rise.
Beavers may explain the river's rise in dragonfly species, but confirming this requires further comparison.

Reid argues that reduced fertilizer runoff, not beaver ponds, explains the rise in dragonfly species.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Refuse heaps, or middens, were once excavated mainly for the intact objects that might be buried in them. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, sprint coaches prescribed long, held stretches before races, reasoning that looser muscles would move faster. Physiologist Dana Okafor tested that reasoning with thirty collegiate sprinters, who ran 40-meter dashes after either five minutes of held stretches or five minutes of leg swings and skips. The results, however, ran counter to the coaches' expectation: the sprinters were, on average, slightly slower after the held stretches. Okafor suggests that holding a stretch may briefly reduce a muscle's springiness, the very quality a sprint start depends on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study compared two five-minute warm-up routines, using thirty collegiate sprinters as its participants.
A study suggests that the held stretches coaches long recommended before sprints may slightly slow sprinters down.
Okafor's study shows that athletes should remove stretching of every kind from their training programs.
Okafor found that held stretches improved sprint times by making the sprinters' leg muscles springier.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the coaches' long-held belief, then uses 'however' to bring in the real finding: held stretches were followed by slightly slower sprints, possibly because they reduce springiness. Choice B covers both the belief and the finding that corrects it, and it keeps the text's hedge ('may').

A.why: This accurately describes how the study was set up, but it leaves out what the study found. You picked a true detail from the middle of the passage instead of the point the whole passage is building toward.

C.why: The study only compared held stretches with leg swings and skips before sprints. It says nothing about getting rid of all stretching, and leg swings are themselves a kind of dynamic stretching. You stretched a narrow finding into a sweeping rule.

D.why: The sprinters were slower after held stretches, and Okafor suggests that stretching reduces springiness. This choice turns both parts of the finding around, so you may have taken the coaches' expectation for the result.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Leaves and wood fossilize only under unusual conditions, so many ancient plants are missing from the record of large fossils. Pollen grains, by contrast, have tough outer walls that survive in ordinary lake mud. At the Harlow Basin site, for instance, paleobotanist Mei Tanaka found abundant pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments, though not a single leaf of that shrub has been found anywhere in the basin. For Tanaka, the pollen fills a gap that the larger fossils leave open.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tanaka found pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments at the Harlow Basin site.
Pollen analysis has made the study of fossil leaves and wood unnecessary for understanding ancient plants.
Pollen grains are fragile, so they survive only in the unusual conditions that also preserve fossil leaves.
Because pollen survives more readily than leaves and wood, it can reveal ancient plants that large fossils miss.
items.explanation: The first two sentences make a general claim: large plant fossils are rare, but pollen survives well. The Harlow Basin case is an example of that claim, and the final sentence says the pollen fills the gap. Choice D states the general claim that the example supports.

A.why: This repeats the Harlow Basin example correctly, but that example only supports the passage's broader point about pollen and the fossil record. You chose the vivid case instead of the claim it illustrates.

B.why: The passage says pollen fills a gap that larger fossils leave. It never says leaves and wood are no longer worth studying. You turned 'adds to' into 'replaces'.

C.why: The passage says pollen has tough walls that survive in ordinary lake mud, and that leaves are the fossils needing unusual conditions. This choice swaps the two.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Some meteorologists have proposed that the heat radiating from large cities may trigger summer thunderstorms downwind. Radar records from the city of Aldermoor appear to fit this idea: storms form noticeably more often just east of the city than to its west. Meteorologist Priya Venkatesan cautions, however, that the prevailing winds also carry moisture from nearby Lake Tessel over the same eastern area. The lake, rather than the city's heat, could therefore account for the pattern, and separating the two influences will require further study.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Radar records fit the idea that city heat triggers storms downwind, but moisture from a lake could also explain them.
Radar records prove that Aldermoor's heat is the main reason summer storms form more often east of the city.
Prevailing summer winds near Aldermoor carry moisture from Lake Tessel over the area east of the city.
Venkatesan rejects the heat hypothesis because storms east of Aldermoor are no more common than elsewhere.
items.explanation: The passage gives a hypothesis and some evidence that fits it, then uses 'however' to bring in a second possible explanation, and ends by saying more study is needed. Choice A covers both the fit and the doubt, and like the text it does not claim certainty.

B.why: The passage says the records 'appear to fit' the idea, and then raises a competing explanation. 'Prove' and 'main reason' are much stronger than the text allows. You missed the hedge words.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it is only one step in the passage's argument. It does not mention the heat hypothesis or the uncertainty the passage is really about.

D.why: The records show storms do form more often east of the city. Venkatesan does not reject the hypothesis either. She only says another cause is possible.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists generally expect a large new employer to push up wages in a small town by competing for workers. Examining warehouse openings in forty rural counties, economist Luis Ferreira found that hourly pay at nearby retailers did rise, by about 4 percent in the first year. Many retail workers soon moved to the warehouses, though, and retailers responded by cutting staff and hours rather than raising pay further. Within three years, retail wages had drifted back close to their earlier levels. Taken together, Ferreira's findings suggest that the wage boost from a new large employer may be real but short-lived.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In the first year after a warehouse opened nearby, hourly pay at local retailers rose by about 4 percent.
Opening a large warehouse is the most effective way for a rural county to raise its long-term wages.
Research suggests that a large new employer may raise local wages at first, but the increase may not last.
Retail wages kept climbing for three years after the warehouses opened, as competition for workers grew.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: an early rise, workers leaving retail jobs, and wages falling back. The last sentence adds them up: the boost is 'real but short-lived.' Choice C restates that conclusion and keeps its hedge.

A.why: This is an accurate statistic from the passage, but it describes only the first year. The passage goes on to show the gain fading. You stopped at one true fact instead of reading through to the final verdict.

B.why: The passage finds that the wage gain faded, and it never compares warehouses with other ways of raising wages. 'Most effective' and 'long-term' are claims the text does not support.

D.why: The passage says retail wages returned close to their earlier levels within three years. This choice reverses what happened after the first year.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Farmers across the Venn Plateau widely credit a drought-tolerant maize variety, introduced in 2015, for the sharp rise in local yields since then. However, when agronomist Hana Brisco compared records from 300 farms, she found that yields rose just as much on farms that kept planting older varieties. The rise instead tracked the spread of no-till planting, a practice that leaves crop residue on fields and helps soil hold moisture. Brisco concludes that soil management, not seed choice, likely drove most of the gains.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The yield rise widely credited to a new maize variety was likely driven more by a change in soil management.
Farms on the Venn Plateau that kept planting older maize varieties also saw their yields rise after 2015.
The drought-tolerant variety performs worse than older varieties, so farmers should stop planting it.
Brisco confirmed that the new maize variety, rather than any change in farming practice, raised yields.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the farmers' belief about why yields rose, then 'However' introduces Brisco's evidence pointing to no-till planting. What comes after the pivot is the author's real point. Choice A states it and keeps the hedge 'likely'.

B.why: This is true, and it is part of Brisco's evidence, but it is only one piece of it. It leaves out the no-till explanation and the conclusion about what caused the gains.

C.why: Brisco found that older varieties did just as well, not better. The passage also never recommends dropping the new seed. You treated 'no extra benefit' as 'harmful'.

D.why: This repeats the farmers' belief, which Brisco's findings go against. You may have read the opening sentence and missed the 'However' turn.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The loss of a single predator can reshape an entire ecosystem. Consider Lake Corvin, where heavy angling during the 1990s removed most of the largemouth bass. Freed from their chief predator, small minnows multiplied rapidly. The minnows, in turn, consumed much of the lake's zooplankton, the tiny animals that had kept algae in check. Within a decade, dense algae blooms had clouded the once-clear water, shading out underwater plants that many other species relied on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Algae bloomed in Lake Corvin after the minnows consumed much of the zooplankton that had grazed on it.
Overfishing of predators is the leading cause of algae blooms in freshwater lakes around the world.
Removing the bass from Lake Corvin had little effect beyond reducing the number of fish anglers caught.
As the case of Lake Corvin shows, losing one predator can set off a chain of changes across an ecosystem.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim, and the rest of the passage traces one example step by step. Choice D states the claim and connects it to the example the passage uses to support it.

A.why: This accurately describes one link near the end of the chain, but it leaves out the predator and the general point the example is meant to show. You picked a vivid detail instead of the passage's claim.

B.why: The passage describes one lake. It never compares causes of algae blooms or makes a claim about lakes worldwide. You turned a single example into a global ranking.

C.why: The passage says removing the bass led to minnow growth, zooplankton loss, algae blooms, and harm to underwater plants. That is far more than 'little effect'.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the mountain village of Ostrava Alta, residents can hold conversations entirely in whistles. Linguist Tomás Reyna has proposed that this whistled speech arose so that shepherds could talk across steep valleys, and his recordings show that the whistles carry about two kilometers, far beyond the reach of shouted words. Yet, as other researchers point out, showing that the system works well over distance does not show why it began. It may have started as a courtship code or a children's game and only later been put to use across the valleys.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recordings show that the whistled speech of Ostrava Alta carries about two kilometers across the valleys.
The whistles' long range shows that they are useful over distance, but not that this is why they began.
The whistles' long range proves that villagers first developed them to speak across the steep valleys.
Shouted words carry farther than whistles, so the whistled speech most likely began as a children's game.
items.explanation: The passage grants that the whistles carry far, then uses 'Yet' to raise the stronger objection: being useful over distance does not explain how the system began. Choice B keeps both the concession and the limit.

A.why: This is an accurate detail from Reyna's recordings, but it is only the evidence the passage goes on to question. It leaves out the passage's point about the difference between usefulness and origin.

C.why: The first half, about long range, is right. The second half claims 'proves', which is exactly the conclusion the passage says the evidence cannot reach. You recognized the opening and stopped reading.

D.why: The recordings show whistles carry farther than shouted words, not the other way around. The passage also offers the game only as a possibility, not the most likely origin.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Histories of the Marren Valley's choral festivals have long credited conductor Elsa Varga with founding the tradition when she organized a gathering of choirs in 1869. However, parish records recently examined by musicologist Iván Kertész describe an earlier festival, held in 1861, at which eleven village choirs sang together under the direction of a network of local schoolteachers. Varga's own letters, Kertész notes, mention that she attended that gathering as a young singer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Varga's letters show that, as a young singer, she attended a festival of eleven village choirs in 1861.
Kertész's research shows that Varga played no meaningful role in the history of the valley's festivals.
Newly examined records suggest the festival tradition began earlier than credited, under local teachers.
The parish records confirm that Varga organized the valley's first choral festival in the year 1869.
items.explanation: The passage presents the accepted credit to Varga, then 'However' brings in records of an earlier festival led by schoolteachers, backed up by Varga's own letters. Choice C states the correction the whole passage builds toward.

A.why: This is true, but it is only the final supporting detail. It leaves out the passage's larger point, which is that the accepted story of how the tradition began is wrong.

B.why: The passage suggests Varga was not the first founder. It never says she was unimportant. She still organized the 1869 gathering. You pushed a narrow correction into a total dismissal.

D.why: The parish records describe an earlier 1861 festival, which challenges the claim that Varga's was the first. You mixed up the old account with what the new evidence shows.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Ekwueme's 2019 novel The Long Rows. Ines, an agricultural researcher, is visiting her test fields after a summer without rain.

Ines had driven out expecting to find nothing. The neighboring farms were brown to the fence line, their corn folded over like paper. But at the edge of her plots she stopped. The wheat she had spent six years crossing and recrossing stood upright, thin but green, its heads already filling. She knelt and pressed a stalk between her fingers, as if to be sure it was real, and found that she was laughing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is relieved to discover that the wheat she developed has survived the drought.
Ines is discouraged to find that her test plots fared no better than nearby farms.
Ines worries that her neighbors will resent the success of her experimental crop.
Ines notices that the corn on neighboring farms has been damaged by the dry summer.
items.explanation: You follow Ines from expecting to find nothing to kneeling in disbelief and laughing. The turn at 'But' shows her wheat has survived when everything around it died, and her laughter shows relief and joy. Choice A matches both the situation and that emotional direction.

B.why: You reversed the tone. Ines expected failure, but the text says her wheat 'stood upright' and green while the nearby farms were brown. Her laughing shows the opposite of discouragement.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Ines is thinking about her neighbors' feelings. Their farms appear only as a contrast to her surviving wheat.

D.why: You picked a true detail from the second sentence, but it is too narrow. The dead corn is background that sets up the real focus: Ines's reaction to her own wheat.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.
Only when I peeled the sheet away
did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the tools and materials needed to cut and ink a woodblock.
The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.
items.explanation: In plain English: the speaker carves 'by feel' with the image held 'backward' in mind, and 'only when' the paper comes off does the heron appear clearly, 'more certain' than the speaker felt. The poem moves from working half-blind to seeing the image revealed, and choice C covers both parts.

A.why: You described only the images from the first lines (the block, the ink, the paper) and missed the turn at 'Only when,' where the poem arrives at its point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The heron faces 'the right way at last.' The print shows what the speaker's hands 'had meant,' so it matches the speaker's intention rather than disappointing it.

D.why: You added a regret the poem never states. The speaker admits to uncertainty but never wishes for a different medium. The ending sounds like wonder, not regret.
