items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Harriet Olumide's 2015 novel Census. Theo, a graduate student in ornithology, is conducting a morning bird count in a marsh.

Theo had been told the count would be tedious: three hours on a wet platform, tallying whatever flew past. By the first hour he had filled two pages. A pair of rails picked through the reeds below him; a harrier swung low over the water and was gone. He forgot the cold in his boots. When his supervisor's truck pulled up, Theo looked at his watch in disbelief. It seemed impossible that the morning was already over.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Theo finds the bird count just as tedious as others had warned him it would be.
Theo becomes so absorbed in the bird count that the morning passes unnoticed.
Theo hopes to impress his supervisor by recording more birds than expected.
Theo watches a harrier fly low over the marsh water before it disappears.
items.explanation: Theo was warned the count would be tedious, but he fills pages, forgets the cold, and can't believe the morning is over. Those are signs of someone absorbed in his work, and choice B captures that.

A.why: You took the warning in the first sentence as Theo's real experience. Everything after it, such as forgetting the cold and his 'disbelief' at the time, shows the count was the opposite of tedious.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. The supervisor shows up only to mark the end of the morning. Nothing says Theo is trying to impress anyone.

D.why: You chose one image from the middle of the passage. The harrier is one of many sights that hold Theo's attention, not the point of the passage.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Ansel Varga's 2021 novel Contour Lines. Lucía, a cartographer, is preparing a new map of the valley where she grew up.

Lucía had drawn hundreds of valleys, but never her own. The survey data arrived on a Tuesday, and she traced it as she would any other: the ridgeline, the river, the new reservoir spreading blue across the lower fields. Only when she began to letter the names did she pause. There was no label to give the square where her grandmother had kept goats, no road to mark to the schoolhouse. The water covered all of it. She set down her pen and did not pick it up again until evening.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lucía is pleased to finally have the chance to map the valley where she grew up.
Lucía leaves the flooded village off the map to avoid upsetting her own family.
Lucía uses survey data to trace the ridgeline and river of a mountain valley.
Lucía is saddened when mapping her home valley shows that familiar places are gone.
items.explanation: Lucía starts out treating the job like any other, then stops when she sees that the places she remembers are under the reservoir. Putting down her pen until evening shows her grief. Choice D matches both the situation and the move toward loss.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The text never shows Lucía pleased. It builds toward her stopping work entirely because of what the water has covered.

B.why: You added a motive and an action the text never gives. The places are missing from the map because they are underwater, not because Lucía chose to hide them from anyone.

C.why: You chose a true description of the routine part of the passage and missed the pause that follows, which is where the passage's meaning lies.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Noor Castellanos's 2017 poem "Gauge." The speaker is a hydrologist who measures a river's height each spring.

Each spring I wade out to the gauge
and read the river by its rising marks,
the numbers climbing inch by inch
with snow that fell on peaks I'll never climb.
I write them down. I send them on.
But this year, standing waist-deep in the cold,
I felt the whole weight of the mountain's winter
pressing past my legs toward the sea,
and then, and only then, I understood
what all my columns had been counting.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker explains the procedure for recording a river's height every spring.
The speaker realizes, while doing a routine task, the force behind the numbers.
The speaker grows tired of measuring a river whose changes seem too small.
The speaker gives up recording data in favor of experiencing the river directly.
items.explanation: In plain English: every year the speaker reads the gauge and passes along the numbers, but this year, feeling the snowmelt push past, the speaker 'then, and only then' understands what those numbers stand for. Choice B includes both the routine and the realization it leads to.

C.why: You reversed the tone. The speaker feels 'the whole weight' of the river, not changes too small to matter, and the poem ends in understanding rather than weariness.

D.why: You added a decision the poem never states. The speaker comes to understand the columns of data. Nothing says the speaker stops keeping them.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Desmond Achterberg's 2012 novel Load Paths. Walter, a retired civil engineer, is being driven across a bridge he helped design forty years earlier.

His granddaughter drove, chatting about her classes, and Walter let her talk. As the car climbed onto the span, he felt the old habit return: he listened for the joints, watched the cables, counted the lamp posts. Every one was where he had put it. Traffic streamed past in both directions, hundreds of people who had never heard his name and never needed to. Walter settled back in his seat and smiled. Forty years, and it was still holding everyone up.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Walter feels quiet pride that the bridge he designed still serves people so well.
Walter is anxious that the aging bridge may no longer be safe for drivers to cross.
Walter is hurt that the people crossing his bridge do not know who designed it.
Walter's granddaughter talks to him about her classes while she drives the car.
items.explanation: Walter checks the bridge out of old habit, finds everything where he put it, then settles back and smiles because it is 'still holding everyone up.' That is quiet pride in lasting work, which is choice A.

B.why: You read his listening and watching as worry. The text calls it 'the old habit,' and what he finds, every part where he put it, leads him to relax and smile rather than feel anxious.

C.why: You added a hurt feeling the text never gives. The drivers 'never needed to' know his name, and Walter smiles right after, so he is content, not wounded.

The following text is from Hollis Arden's 2017 poem "To a First-Year Grower." The speaker addresses a new farmer.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To lament the many seasons the speaker spent doubting whether the beans would grow

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Greta Lindqvist's 2008 memoir Leaf Beds. The narrator recalls her first fossil-collecting trip with her father, a paleobotanist.

My father split shale the way other fathers carved roasts, with ceremony and a running commentary. I was nine and had come along mostly for the sandwiches. Then he handed me the hammer, and the slab I struck fell open on a fern frond, every vein intact, pressed there some three hundred million years before anyone had a name for ferns. I did not hear what he said next. I only remember thinking that the rock had been keeping a secret, and that I had been the one it chose to tell.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the father's pride as he watches his daughter uncover her very first fossil
To explain how paleobotanists estimate the age of fern fossils preserved in shale
To show that the narrator decided on this trip to become a paleobotanist herself
To convey the narrator's sense of wonder at the moment she first found a fossil herself
items.explanation: The memoir centers on the narrator as a child. She starts out uninterested ('mostly for the sandwiches'), then splits open a perfect fern and is so absorbed that she doesn't hear her father. She feels the rock 'chose to tell' her its secret. The excerpt conveys her wonder at that first discovery.

A.why: This is the wrong-person trap. The narrator says she 'did not hear what he said next,' so the text never shows how her father reacted. The focus is on what she felt.

B.why: The text gives an age of about three hundred million years but never says how anyone worked it out. You've credited the excerpt with a method it doesn't describe.

C.why: The moment clearly affected her, but the text never says she decided on a career. This choice adds a consequence the excerpt doesn't give.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Idris Calloway's 2019 novel The Surveyor's Daughter. In the 1880s, Nell is helping her father complete a map of a river valley.

Each evening Nell inked the day's measurements onto the sheet: the bend where the river doubled back, the ford, the stand of cottonwoods the survey party had camped beneath. A map, her father liked to say, is a promise that a place will stay where you left it. Nell wanted that promise to be true. Yet as the blank spaces filled, she found herself missing them, the way she might miss a question once it had been answered, and she lingered over the last empty corner before she let herself draw it in.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey the father's belief that careful mapmaking is the most valuable kind of work
To portray Nell's mixed feelings as the map she is helping create nears completion
To describe the route the survey party followed as it traveled through the river valley
To suggest that Nell leaves part of the map unfinished to preserve the valley's mystery
items.explanation: Nell is the focus. She wants the map's 'promise' to hold, but after 'Yet' she admits she misses the blank spaces and hesitates over the last corner before filling it in. The excerpt shows her feeling torn as the map nears completion.

A.why: This shifts the focus to the father and overstates his view. He calls a map a promise but never ranks mapmaking above other work, and his saying is there to set up Nell's feelings.

C.why: The bend, the ford, and the cottonwoods are incidental details. The text never lays out a route, and this choice ignores Nell's feelings, which are what the excerpt is about.

D.why: Nell lingers over the last corner, but the text says she does 'draw it in' at the end. She doesn't leave any part of the map unfinished.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Collagraphy is a printmaking method in which textured materials are glued onto a board, inked, and pressed onto paper. It has often been treated as a classroom exercise rather than a serious medium. Yet Brazilian artist Tereza Moraes has built a three-decade career around it. Moraes layers fishing net, sand, and torn cardboard onto her plates, producing prints whose ridges can be felt as well as seen. Because the fragile surfaces wear down after five or six impressions, her editions are unusually small, and collectors now seek them out.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why Moraes's collagraph plates wear down after only five or six impressions
To introduce an artist who has built a serious career on a method often seen as elementary
To argue that art schools should teach collagraphy instead of more traditional printmaking methods
To contrast the materials Moraes uses with those favored by earlier collagraph artists
items.explanation: Every sentence serves one profile. The text defines collagraphy, notes that people often treat it as a classroom exercise, and then turns with 'Yet' to Moraes, whose long career, distinctive plates, and sought-after editions show the method used seriously. Choice B covers that whole arc, and 'introduce' matches the text's neutral, informative tone.

A.why: You picked a true detail. The plates do wear down quickly, but that is one supporting fact in a text about Moraes and her career, not the purpose of the whole passage.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text never recommends anything to art schools. It describes an artist and does not argue for a change in curriculum.

D.why: You brought in a comparison the text doesn't make. No earlier collagraph artists are mentioned, so the text cannot be contrasting Moraes's materials with theirs.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. Streams are not fixed in one category, though: a stream can shift between gaining and losing as the water table around it rises and falls. The Arroyo Pinto in northern Mexico is a case in point. During the summer rains, groundwater near its channel sits high enough to seep into the stream. By late winter, the surrounding aquifer has dropped so far that the arroyo's water drains downward, and the channel runs dry within a few kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain a hydrological category and show how a single stream can move in and out of it
To describe the summer rains that raise groundwater levels near the Arroyo Pinto each year
To argue that losing streams are more vulnerable to drought than hydrologists have assumed
To show that the Arroyo Pinto remains a losing stream during every season of the year
items.explanation: The text defines a 'losing stream,' states the general rule that streams can switch between gaining and losing, and then uses the Arroyo Pinto to illustrate that rule. Choice A covers the definition, the rule, and the example together.

B.why: You chose one real detail. The summer rains appear only as part of the example, and the text is about the stream's changing relationship to groundwater, not about the rains.

C.why: You read in an argument the text never makes. It says nothing about drought vulnerability or about what hydrologists have wrongly assumed. It only explains and illustrates.

D.why: You reversed the example. In summer, groundwater seeps into the Arroyo Pinto, so it is gaining then. It becomes a losing stream only in late winter.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. However, specimens recovered in 2019 preserve small seeds attached to the leaf bases, and ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds. Those seeds have thick protective coats, and the plant's leaves grew in tight, leathery clusters. Together, these features have led paleobotanists to reclassify Velatophyllum as an early seed plant, one apparently suited to surviving long, dark polar winters.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why ferns reproduce by spores rather than by producing seeds on their leaves
To argue that most plant fossils found in Antarctica have been misidentified by researchers
To describe how new specimens changed scientists' view of what kind of plant a fossil was
To show that the 2019 specimens confirmed that Velatophyllum was an unusual kind of fern
items.explanation: The text opens with a long-held assumption that Velatophyllum was a fern, turns on 'However' to the 2019 seed-bearing specimens, and ends with the plant's reclassification. Choice C covers that old-view-to-new-view structure for the fossil as a whole.

A.why: You picked a supporting fact. The point about spores is there only to show why seeds rule out a fern. It is a step in the reasoning, not the text's purpose.

B.why: You generalized beyond the text. It discusses one misidentified fossil and says nothing about most Antarctic plant fossils, and it doesn't argue a broad claim.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. The 2019 specimens overturned the fern classification rather than confirming it, and Velatophyllum was reclassified as a seed plant.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. For decades, however, they could be produced only as thin ribbons or small pieces, because thicker samples cooled too slowly at their centers and crystallized. Engineer Hana Okafor's team has now developed an iron-based alloy that stays glassy at thicknesses of several centimeters. Its first commercial use, in springs for precision watches, exploits the material's ability to flex millions of times without permanently deforming.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why rapid cooling keeps the atoms in certain alloys from arranging into crystals
To argue that metallic glasses will soon replace steel in most kinds of industrial manufacturing
To show that metallic glasses are weaker than ordinary metals but far more flexible than them
To describe a class of materials, a long-standing obstacle to making them, and a recent advance
items.explanation: The text moves in three steps. It says what metallic glasses are, then explains why they long couldn't be made thick ('however'), then presents Okafor's alloy and its first use. Choice D names those three parts in the order the text gives them.

A.why: You chose a true detail from the opening sentence. Rapid cooling is part of the definition, but the text goes on to cover a manufacturing limit and a breakthrough, which this choice leaves out.

B.why: You chose a verb and a claim that are too strong. The text mentions a single use in watch springs and makes no prediction about replacing steel.

C.why: You misread the properties. The text calls metallic glasses 'unusually strong,' not weaker than ordinary metals.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: City planners usually treat alleys as service corridors, places for trash bins and delivery trucks rather than for people. Kellbrook's Green Alley Program, launched in 2012, takes a different view. The program replaces cracked asphalt with permeable pavers that let rainwater soak into the soil, adds lighting and planters, and invites residents on each block to vote on features such as benches or murals. More than ninety of the city's alleys have now been converted, and several host weekend markets.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how permeable pavers reduce the amount of rainwater that flows into city drains
To describe a city program that treats alleys as public spaces rather than as service routes
To argue that other cities should adopt Kellbrook's approach to redesigning their alleys
To show that Kellbrook's alleys are still used mainly for trash collection and deliveries
items.explanation: After a brief note on how alleys are usually treated, the rest of the text describes the Green Alley Program: what it changes, how residents take part, and what has come of it. Choice B covers the whole text, and 'describe' fits its informative tone.

A.why: You picked a single feature. Permeable pavers are one element of the program, and the text doesn't explain drainage in any detail. It is profiling the program as a whole.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text reports what Kellbrook has done but never recommends the program to other cities.

D.why: You reversed the text. It describes how the program moved alleys away from purely service use, noting that ninety have been converted and some now host markets.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Musicologists long regarded the Ferrand Songbook, a manuscript of forty-eight part-songs from the 1590s, as the careful work of a single copyist. Close study of its ink and handwriting, however, has revealed at least four different hands. Several songs also appear twice, the second version apparently corrected after being performed. Scholars now describe the songbook not as a finished anthology but as a working collection, added to and revised by a circle of musicians over perhaps two decades.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how the study of ink and handwriting helps scholars date musical manuscripts
To argue that the Ferrand Songbook is the most important surviving set of 1590s part-songs
To describe how scholars have come to see a manuscript as a shared and evolving collection
To show that the Ferrand Songbook's songs were copied once and never revised afterward
items.explanation: The text presents the old view of the songbook as one copyist's work, turns on 'however' to the evidence of several hands and revised songs, and ends with the new view of a collaborative working collection. Choice C covers that whole shift.

A.why: You focused on the method rather than the subject. The ink and handwriting study is mentioned only as the source of the new evidence, and the text never discusses dating manuscripts.

B.why: You chose a claim the text never makes. It doesn't rank the songbook against other collections or argue for its importance.

D.why: You reversed the evidence. The text says several songs appear in a second, corrected version and that the collection was revised over decades.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: In some languages, a speaker cannot simply report that something happened; the grammar itself requires the speaker to indicate how they know it. Linguists call this feature evidentiality. In Tamuri, a language spoken by about 12,000 people in the Andean highlands, one verb suffix marks events the speaker witnessed, another marks events learned from others, and a third marks conclusions drawn from clues, such as wet ground indicating rain. Leaving the suffix off is not an option: a Tamuri sentence without one is ungrammatical.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a grammatical feature and illustrate it with a language that requires its use
To explain how Tamuri speakers conclude from wet ground that rain must have fallen
To argue that languages with evidentiality let speakers communicate more accurately
To show that Tamuri speakers may decide for themselves whether to mark their sources
items.explanation: The text begins with a general statement that some grammars require speakers to mark how they know something, names that feature evidentiality, and then uses Tamuri's three suffixes as a concrete example. Choice A covers both the general feature and the illustration.

B.why: You picked the most vivid detail. The wet-ground example only illustrates one of Tamuri's three suffixes and is not what the text as a whole is about.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text explains the feature neutrally and never claims it makes communication more accurate.

D.why: You missed the final sentence. It says leaving the suffix off is 'not an option,' so marking the source is required, not optional.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Surviving weavers' pattern books usually preserve textile designs but reveal little about the people who made them. The notebooks of Scottish weaver Janet Rennick (1821–1894) are an exception. Alongside samples of her checked woolens, Rennick recorded the price of each batch of yarn, the names of the neighbors who spun it, and the days her loom stood idle when dye shipments ran late. Historians have used the notebooks to reconstruct how a rural weaving household earned and lost money as factory cloth flooded local markets.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the checked woolen patterns that Rennick wove for customers in her village
To argue that the spread of factory cloth drove rural weaving households into poverty
To show that Rennick's notebooks, like most pattern books, contain only design samples
To describe a weaver's records and explain why they are valuable to historians of work
items.explanation: The text contrasts typical pattern books with Rennick's notebooks, lists what she recorded beyond designs, and ends with how historians have used those records. Choice D covers both what the notebooks contain and why they matter.

A.why: You chose a detail that really is in the text but is too narrow. The woolen samples are mentioned in passing, and the text's interest is in the business records kept alongside them.

B.why: You went beyond the text. It says the notebooks show how one household earned and lost money, and it doesn't argue that factory cloth impoverished rural weavers in general.

C.why: You reversed the text's central contrast. The notebooks are called 'an exception' because they record far more than designs.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Ecologists have traditionally assumed that earthworms in northern hardwood forests benefit tree seedlings by speeding the release of nutrients from fallen leaves. To test this assumption, ecologist Mireille Okafor fenced forty forest plots, removed the worms from half of them, and tracked sugar maple seedlings in every plot for three years. Seedlings in the worm-free plots survived at nearly twice the rate of those in plots with worms, a difference Okafor attributes to the worms' consumption of the leaf litter that shelters young roots.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a study whose results challenge a common assumption about how earthworms affect forest seedlings
To describe a study that could not determine whether earthworms affect the survival of forest seedlings
To compare the effects of earthworms on sugar maple seedlings with their effects on other tree species
To argue that earthworms should be removed from northern hardwood forests in order to protect seedlings
items.explanation: The text opens with what ecologists have 'traditionally assumed' (worms help seedlings), then describes Okafor's experiment, and ends with a clear result: seedlings survived better without worms. So the text reports a study whose findings go against the old assumption. Choice A says both parts: it describes a study, and the study challenges the assumption.

B.why: You saw that the text describes a study and stopped reading the choice there. The last sentence gives a clear result (nearly twice the survival rate), so the question was not left unanswered.

C.why: You assumed the text compares things because it mentions a specific species. Only sugar maples are studied, and no other tree species is mentioned.

D.why: You treated a reported finding as a recommendation. The text describes what Okafor found. It never argues that anyone should remove worms from forests.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Folklorists have long debated whether the tale of the clever miller spread through southern Europe by word of mouth or through cheap printed chapbooks. To address the question, folklorist Tomasz Rędzik catalogued 214 recorded versions of the tale, noting each storyteller's village and the date the version was collected. Versions told far from any printing town often kept the same rare plot details found in chapbook texts, but only when the teller's village lay on a major trade road, a pattern Rędzik reads as evidence that traveling peddlers carried printed copies inland.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how a folklorist used the locations of recorded versions of a tale to address how that tale spread
To argue that oral storytelling played no role in preserving traditional tales anywhere in southern Europe
To describe a catalog of versions of a tale that left the question of how the tale spread unresolved
To contrast the plot details found in chapbook texts with those found in versions told in printing towns
items.explanation: The text sets up an open question (did the tale spread orally or in print?), then describes Rędzik's method of recording where each version came from, and ends with the pattern he found and how he interprets it. Choice A covers that whole arc: a method based on the locations of versions, used to answer a question about how the tale spread.

B.why: You stretched one finding about one tale into a sweeping claim. The text links printed copies to certain villages on trade roads. It says nothing about oral storytelling playing 'no role' anywhere.

C.why: You matched the opening verb and missed the result. The last sentence reports a clear pattern and Rędzik's interpretation of it, so the question was not left open.

D.why: You picked out one comparison of plot details and treated it as the point of the whole text. That comparison is one piece of evidence, and the versions it involves were told far from printing towns, not in them.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Most earthquakes release built-up stress within seconds. Along some subduction zones, however, the boundary between two plates can slip over weeks without producing strong shaking. In these slow slip events, fluids squeezed out of the descending plate collect along the fault and reduce the friction that normally locks the plates together. The plates then creep past each other a few centimeters at a time, and that movement can transfer stress to neighboring, still-locked segments of the fault, which may later rupture in ordinary earthquakes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how slow slip events occur and how they can affect nearby segments of a fault
To compare how often slow slip events and ordinary earthquakes occur along subduction zones
To describe how fluids are first formed deep within plates that are sinking at subduction zones
To question the view that slow slip events can add stress to neighboring segments of a fault
items.explanation: After the 'however,' the text walks through a process step by step: fluids collect, friction drops, the plates creep, and stress moves to neighboring fault segments. It explains and doesn't judge. Choice A names the whole process, from its cause to its effect on nearby segments.

B.why: You took the brief contrast in the first sentence as a comparison the whole text is built on. The text explains only slow slip events and never says how often either kind of event happens.

C.why: You focused on one step. The text says the fluids are squeezed out of the plate but doesn't explain how they form, and that step is only the start of the process the text describes.

D.why: You assumed the text evaluates when it only explains. It states directly that slow slip can transfer stress to neighboring segments, so it supports this view rather than questioning it.

items.stimulus: Nineteenth-century mapmakers often showed mountain slopes with hachures, short lines drawn more thickly on steeper ground. To describe a comparison that confirmed scholars' view that hachures recorded slope only roughly

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Hydrologists have long relied on rainfall totals to forecast floods, but in mountain basins during winter, rain alone can be a poor guide. When warm rain falls on a deep snowpack, the snow at first absorbs the water much as a sponge would, and little runoff reaches nearby streams. Once the pack becomes saturated, however, it can release both the stored rain and its own meltwater at once, so stream levels may surge hours after the storm itself has peaked.

To explain how warm rain melts a deep snowpack, a process that keeps mountain basins from flooding
To compare the methods used to forecast floods in mountain basins with the methods used in lowlands
To argue that hydrologists should stop using rainfall totals altogether when they forecast floods
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a claim (rainfall totals can be a poor guide), and the rest explains the process behind it: the snowpack absorbs rain, becomes saturated, and then releases everything at once, well after the storm. Choice A connects the claim to the whole process.

B.why: You stopped at the first step of the process. The snowpack does hold water back at first, but the text goes on to say it then releases a surge, so the process leads to flooding instead of preventing it.

C.why: You expected a comparison the text doesn't make. Only mountain basins are discussed, and lowland forecasting is never mentioned.

D.why: You turned a limit into a rejection. The text says rainfall 'alone' can mislead in one setting. It never says hydrologists should abandon rainfall totals entirely.

items.stimulus: It has been unclear why some asteroids in the outer main belt look redder than their neighbors. Their surfaces might be made of different material, or they might simply have been exposed to space radiation for longer. To describe a study suggesting that all red objects in the solar system share the same unusual composition

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Marine biologists have typically assumed that a sea star that loses an arm must divert energy away from reproduction in order to regrow the limb. To test this, biologist Kaito Mercer removed one arm from each of 60 sea stars in aquarium tanks and compared them with 60 uninjured animals over a full spawning season. The injured animals regrew their arms yet produced as many eggs as the uninjured ones did; they instead ate about 30 percent more food, suggesting that they met the extra energy demand by increasing their intake.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To describe an experiment indicating that injured sea stars pay for regrowing lost arms by producing fewer eggs
To explain how sea stars regrow a lost arm by forming new tissue at the site where the injury occurred
To describe an experiment indicating that sea stars in aquariums regrow lost arms faster than wild sea stars
items.explanation: The text states an assumption (regrowth costs reproduction), describes Mercer's experiment, and reports a result that goes against the assumption: egg production held steady while food intake rose. Choice A gets both the experiment and its finding right.

B.why: You chose the assumption the text sets out to test instead of what the experiment found. The injured sea stars produced as many eggs as the uninjured ones.

C.why: You assumed the text explains how regrowth works. It says the arms regrew but never describes how new tissue forms. It is about the energy cost of regrowth.

D.why: You brought in a comparison the study never made. All the sea stars were in aquarium tanks, and no wild animals were measured.

Night after night Lena kept her watch at the eyepiece, wrapped in a blanket against the cold, patient as a heron standing in a shallow pond. The neighbors' lights went out one by one. Then, a little before dawn on the ninth night, the comet swam into view at last, faint and pale, trailing its thin hair of light across the stars.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "watch" most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Lena stays at the eyepiece night after night, "patient as a heron," waiting for the comet. "Watch" here means a long period of attentive waiting, which is a vigil.

B.why: You picked the most common meaning of "watch," a clock worn on the wrist. The line is about Lena patiently waiting, not about something she wears.

C.why: You were thinking of a weather or storm "watch." Nobody in the passage is being warned about anything.

D.why: She does return every night, but the text describes patient waiting, not a planned timetable. "Kept her schedule at the eyepiece" loses the heron comparison.

items.subtype_name: “Most nearly mean” in a literary excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a story about a farmer testing new soil treatments.

Maria walked the rows at dawn, stooping every few steps to turn a leaf over in her fingers. Her grandfather had taught her to read a field the way a doctor reads a patient. A yellow edge on a corn leaf meant hunger, usually for nitrogen; a curled, papery tip meant thirst. By the third row she knew which plots would need feeding before the week was out.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "hunger" most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The phrase right after the word, "usually for nitrogen," tells you what the plant is missing. In this line, "hunger" means a lack of a nutrient, which is a deficiency.

B.why: You used the ordinary meaning of "hunger," a feeling of wanting food. A leaf has no feelings. The line is about what the plant is short of.

C.why: Famine means a widespread food shortage among people. One yellow leaf edge tells Maria that one plant is short of nitrogen, which is much less than that.

D.why: Greed is a moral fault, wanting more than you need. The plant is lacking something it needs, which is the opposite idea.

items.subtype_name: “Most nearly mean” in a literary excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a story about a mapmaker.

The old surveyor unrolled the chart across the table and smoothed its curling corners with his palms. Along the coast the ink was dark and confident, every cove and headland carefully named. But a few miles inland the lines grew timid, thinning into faint dotted guesses, and then they stopped altogether. Beyond them lay only blank paper and a single word: Unknown.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "timid" most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The inland lines are contrasted with the coast's "dark and confident" ink, and they thin into "faint dotted guesses." So "timid" describes lines drawn with uncertainty, which is tentative.

B.why: You took "timid" literally, as a feeling of fear. Lines on paper can't be afraid. The word describes how faint and unsure the drawing is.

C.why: The lines thin out and then stop, and blank paper comes after them. That is the opposite of crowded.

D.why: The passage contrasts sure lines with unsure ones, not plain lines with decorated ones. "Faint dotted guesses" are not fancy.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a story set in a mill town.

At the mill gate the workers stood in the cold and compared their pay envelopes. Wages had not moved in three years, though the price of bread and coal had climbed steadily all the while, so that each Friday the same coins bought a little less than they had the Friday before, and the envelopes grew lighter in every sense but weight.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "moved" most nearly mean?

C.why: You picked the emotional meaning ("the story moved me"). The workers may well be upset, but here the word describes what the wages did, not how anyone felt.

D.why: Nothing in the passage is about convincing anyone. "Wages had not been persuaded" doesn't make sense in the line.

items.stimulus: Arctic terns make one of the longest migrations of any animal, traveling each year between Arctic breeding grounds and Antarctic waters. The observation that such children often combine the grammar of one language with the vocabulary of the ______ taken as proof that they could not keep the two systems apart. Later studies showed the opposite: switches occur at predictable points, which suggests that these speakers command both grammars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is 'The observation that such children often combine the grammar of one language with the vocabulary of the other,' and its verb is 'was taken.' The 'that' clause is part of the subject because it says which observation is meant. A subject is never separated from its verb, so no punctuation is needed.

B.why: The subject ends a long 'that' clause, so it felt as if something needed closing. No comma opened this clause, so there is nothing to close, and one comma between a subject and its verb is incorrect.

C.why: You used a semicolon, which needs a complete sentence on each side. The first side is only a subject, and 'was taken as proof...' has no subject of its own.

D.why: You used a dash to mark the end of the long subject. A single dash needs a complete sentence before it, and this one would separate the subject from its verb.

items.stimulus: Planting two crops together in the same field, a practice called intercropping, can reduce a farm's need for fertilizer. Over four growing seasons, agronomists at a research station in Manitoba grew oats alongside field peas, whose roots host bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air. Compared with oats planted alone, the mixture gave ______ 18 percent more total grain per hectare while requiring no added nitrogen.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: 'Gave' takes two objects here. 'Farmers' is who received something, and 'roughly 18 percent more total grain' is what they received. No punctuation goes between a verb and its objects, so both run straight on from 'gave.'

A.why: The number felt like a new unit, so you paused before it. A comma here separates 'gave farmers' from what the farmers were given, splitting the verb from its object.

B.why: You used a colon to introduce the result. A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and 'the mixture gave farmers' is incomplete because it never says what was given.

C.why: You used a semicolon, which needs a complete sentence on each side. 'Roughly 18 percent more total grain...' has no verb, and the clause before it is missing its object.

In most of them, she outwits a greedy landlord with the help of an animal companion. items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
A hydrologist models the depths of two drainage channels during a storm. In the models below, $x$ is the time in hours since the rain began and $y$ is the depth in centimeters.

$y = \frac{2}{3}x + 5$

$kx - 6y = 12$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Put the second equation in slope-intercept form. $kx - 6y = 12$ becomes $6y = kx - 12$, so $y = \frac{k}{6}x - 2$. For no solution, the slopes must be equal: $\frac{k}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$, so $k = 4$. Now check the intercepts. They are $5$ and $-2$, which are different, so the lines are parallel and never meet. The system has no solution when $k = 4$.

A.why: You compared the slopes before rearranging the second equation properly. You read the slope of $kx - 6y = 12$ as $\frac{k}{-6}$ instead of $\frac{k}{6}$, which gave the wrong sign. That is the trap of comparing an equation in $y = mx + b$ form with one that has not been rearranged.

B.why: $\frac{2}{3}$ is the slope the second line needs. The question asks for $k$, and $k$ is 6 times that slope.

D.why: You wrote the slope of the second line as $\frac{6}{k}$ instead of $\frac{k}{6}$. Solving $\frac{6}{k} = \frac{2}{3}$ gives 9, but with $k = 9$ the slope is $\frac{3}{2}$ and the lines cross.

items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
A meteorology student writes a linear relationship between $x$, the wind speed in meters per second at a coastal station, and $y$, the wind speed in meters per second at an inland station.

$4x - 6y = 10$
items.stem: One of the two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has no solution. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?
items.explanation: Multiply $-2x + 3y = 5$ by $-2$ to get $4x - 6y = -10$. The left side is the same as the given equation's, so the slopes are equal. The right side is $-10$, not $10$, so the lines are different. Parallel, distinct lines never meet, so the system has no solution.

A.why: Multiplying the given equation by $\frac{3}{2}$ gives exactly $6x - 9y = 15$. That is the same line, so the system has infinitely many solutions, not none. You checked that the slopes match but not that the constants are out of ratio.

B.why: The coefficients are in proportion, but the sign of the $y$-term flipped. This line has slope $-\frac{2}{3}$ while the given line has slope $\frac{2}{3}$, so the lines cross once.

C.why: You swapped the coefficients of $x$ and $y$. This line has slope $\frac{3}{2}$, not $\frac{2}{3}$, so it crosses the given line at one point.

items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
An astronomy student models the apparent brightness of two variable stars. In the models, $x$ and $y$ are brightness readings taken with two different filters.

$\frac{1}{2}x - \frac{3}{4}y = 5$

$kx - 9y = 20$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Clear the fractions by multiplying the first equation by 4: $2x - 3y = 20$. For the lines to be parallel, the coefficients must be in proportion. The $y$-coefficient goes from $-3$ to $-9$, a factor of 3, so $k = 3 \cdot 2 = 6$. Check the constants: 3 times the first equation gives $6x - 9y = 60$, and $60 \neq 20$. The lines are distinct, so the system has no solution.

B.why: You made a sign error when you set up the proportion, as if $-9$ divided by $-3$ were $-3$. With $k = -6$ the slopes have opposite signs and the lines cross.

C.why: After scaling the first equation to $2x - 3y = 20$, you matched it to the second equation by its constant, 20, instead of by its $y$-coefficient. So you copied $k = 2$ unchanged. The $y$-coefficients are $-3$ and $-9$, so the $x$-coefficient must also be tripled.

D.why: 3 is the scale factor between the two equations, not $k$. Stopping there leaves out the last step, multiplying the $x$-coefficient 2 by 3.

items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
A paleobotanist models the relationship between $x$, the depth in meters of a sediment layer, and $y$, the number of fossil pollen grains per gram found in that layer.

$y = -\frac{3}{5}x + 4$
items.stem: One of the two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has no solution. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?
items.explanation: Rearrange $3x + 5y = 15$: $5y = -3x + 15$, so $y = -\frac{3}{5}x + 3$. The slope matches the given line, $-\frac{3}{5}$, but the $y$-intercept is 3 instead of 4. The lines are parallel and distinct, so the system has no solution.

B.why: $3x + 5y = 20$ rearranges to $y = -\frac{3}{5}x + 4$, which is the given line. Identical lines give infinitely many solutions. The intercept has to be different too.

C.why: You put the 5 on $x$ and the 3 on $y$. This line has slope $-\frac{5}{3}$, so it crosses the given line once.

D.why: The minus sign in front of $5y$ makes the slope $+\frac{3}{5}$. The given slope is $-\frac{3}{5}$, so the lines cross. The signs matter when you move from $y = mx + b$ form to standard form.

items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
A materials scientist models two properties of an experimental alloy, where $x$ is the percent of nickel and $y$ is the percent of chromium.

$3x - 2y = 8$

$ax - 6y = b$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $a$ and $b$ are constants. If the system has no solution, which of the following could be the values of $a$ and $b$?
items.explanation: The $y$-coefficient goes from $-2$ to $-6$, a factor of 3. For parallel lines the $x$-coefficient must also triple, so $a = 9$. If $b$ were $3 \cdot 8 = 24$, the lines would be identical, so $b$ must be some other number. With $a = 9$ and $b = 20$, the lines are parallel and distinct, so there is no solution.

A.why: $9x - 6y = 24$ is exactly 3 times the first equation. It is the same line, so there are infinitely many solutions. Tripling the constant as well is the trap. It must not be in the same ratio.

C.why: With $a = -9$, the second line has slope $-\frac{3}{2}$ while the first has slope $\frac{3}{2}$. The lines cross once, so there is a solution.

D.why: You doubled the $x$-coefficient and the constant but ignored that the $y$-coefficient tripled. $6x - 6y = 16$ has slope 1, not $\frac{3}{2}$, so the lines intersect.

items.stimulus:
A folklore studies researcher models how two versions of a folktale spread, where $x$ is the number of decades since the tale was first recorded and $y$ is the number of villages where a version is told.

$2y = 5x - 7$

$kx - 4y = 9$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The first equation gives $y = \frac{5}{2}x - \frac{7}{2}$. The second gives $4y = kx - 9$, so $y = \frac{k}{4}x - \frac{9}{4}$. Setting the slopes equal, $\frac{k}{4} = \frac{5}{2}$, so $k = 10$. The intercepts, $-\frac{7}{2}$ and $-\frac{9}{4}$, are different, so the lines are parallel and distinct and the system has no solution.

A.why: $\frac{5}{2}$ is the slope both lines must share. $k$ is the $x$-coefficient in the second equation, which is 4 times that slope.

B.why: You lost a sign when moving terms across the equals sign. The first equation rearranges to $5x - 2y = 7$. Doubling it gives $10x - 4y = 14$, so $k$ is $+10$. With $-10$ the slopes have opposite signs.

C.why: You matched the $x$-coefficients directly even though the equations are in different forms. The $y$-coefficient doubles from $-2$ to $-4$, so the $x$-coefficient must double too. With $k = 5$ the slope is $\frac{5}{4}$ and the lines cross.

items.subtype_name: No solution (parallel, distinct lines)
items.stimulus:
A textile historian models the output of two weaving workshops, where $x$ is the number of bolts of linen and $y$ is the number of bolts of wool produced in a season.

$\frac{x}{4} + \frac{y}{6} = 1$

$3x + ky = 5$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Multiply the first equation by 12 to clear the fractions: $3x + 2y = 12$. The $x$-coefficient already matches the second equation, so parallel lines need $k = 2$. The equations are then $3x + 2y = 12$ and $3x + 2y = 5$. Subtracting gives $0 = 7$, which is false, so the system has no solution.

A.why: You made a sign error. Both $y$-terms are positive, so $k$ must be positive. With $k = -2$ the slopes have opposite signs and the lines cross.

B.why: $\frac{2}{3}$ is the ratio of the $y$-coefficient to the $x$-coefficient after you clear the fractions. The $x$-coefficient in the second equation is 3, so $k$ must be $3 \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 2$.

D.why: You read $\frac{x}{4} + \frac{y}{6}$ as $4x + 6y$ and solved $\frac{k}{3} = \frac{6}{4}$. Dividing by 4 is multiplying by $\frac{1}{4}$, so the coefficients are in the ratio $\frac{1}{4} : \frac{1}{6}$, which is $3 : 2$.

items.subtype_name: Participle in a supplementary phrase (don't add a second verb)
items.stimulus: Inulin occurs naturally in onions, garlic, and bananas, but only in small amounts. Commercial inulin, a soluble fiber ______ chiefly from chicory root and valued by manufacturers for its mild sweetness, now appears in products ranging from yogurt to granola bars, where it can replace some of the sugar and fat without noticeably changing texture.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the main clause is "Commercial inulin," and its main verb, "appears," comes later in the sentence. The blank sits inside the appositive "a soluble fiber ______ chiefly from chicory root," which describes the fiber. That phrase needs a modifier, not a second tensed verb. The fiber receives the action (someone extracts it), so you need the past participle "extracted."

B.why: You saw that "is extracted" sounds complete next to "a soluble fiber." But it puts a tensed verb inside the appositive with no "that" or "which" to introduce it, so the sentence falls apart before it reaches the real main verb, "appears."

C.why: You probably picked this because you thought the sentence still needed a verb. It already has one, "appears," further on. "Has been extracted" adds a second tensed verb with no conjunction or relative pronoun to connect it.

D.why: You were right to choose a participle, but you chose the wrong one. "Extracting" makes the fiber do the extracting. The fiber is what gets extracted, so the passive "-ed" form is required.

items.subtype_name: Participle in a supplementary phrase (don't add a second verb)
items.stimulus: In 2019, planners in the river city of Carrow began replacing two traffic lanes along its main commercial street with tree-lined walkways and planted medians. Over the next three years, the new canopy shaded most of the remaining pavement, ______ midsummer surface temperatures along the corridor by an average of 2°C.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause, "the new canopy shaded most of the remaining pavement," already has its subject and verb. What follows the comma describes the result of that shading, so it should be a modifier. Here the shading causes the cooling, so the "-ing" participle "lowering" correctly attaches the result to the clause.

B.why: "It lowered midsummer surface temperatures" is an independent clause. Joining it to another independent clause with only a comma creates a comma splice.

C.why: "Lowers" is a tensed verb with no conjunction to join it to "shaded." It also switches to the present tense in a passage about 2019 to 2022.

items.stimulus: Most vaccines teach the immune system to recognize a threat by exposing it to a weakened or inactivated version of the entire pathogen, so the body encounters dozens of the microbe's surface proteins at once. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: There are two subjects here: most vaccines, which present the whole pathogen and many proteins, and subunit vaccines, which present a single protein. The subjects differ and the attribute flips from many to one. That is a comparison-contrast relationship, so you need 'by contrast.'

A.why: You saw a specific kind of vaccine come after a general statement and took it as an illustration. Subunit vaccines go against the tendency described in the first sentence, because they do not use the whole pathogen. A case that breaks the general claim cannot be an example of it.

B.why: 'Similarly' needs the two subjects to share an attribute. A single purified protein is the opposite of 'dozens of surface proteins,' so the two sentences point in different directions.

D.why: You read a cause-and-effect link that the text does not contain. Whole-pathogen vaccines do not cause subunit vaccines to hold a single protein. The two are simply set side by side as different approaches.

items.subtype_name: Two things set side by side (By contrast / Conversely)
items.stimulus: P waves, the fastest seismic waves an earthquake produces, compress and stretch rock along their direction of travel and can pass through both the solid and the liquid layers of Earth's interior. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The two sentences use the same frame for two kinds of wave. P waves move along the direction of travel and pass through liquid. S waves move perpendicular to it and cannot pass through liquid. The subjects differ and the key attribute flips, so 'in contrast' is correct.

A.why: 'Similarly' only works if S waves share the attribute given for P waves. P waves cross liquid and S waves cannot, so the two are opposites, not parallels.

B.why: S waves are not a sample of P waves or of anything the first sentence describes. They are a second, separate category with the opposite behavior. You treated a specific item as an illustration without checking whether it agrees with what came before.

C.why: P waves' ability to cross liquid does not make S waves move perpendicular or stop at liquid. The passage compares two wave types. It does not describe one causing the other.

items.subtype_name: Two things set side by side (By contrast / Conversely)
items.stimulus: Coaches in most endurance sports have their athletes taper, sharply cutting training volume in the final weeks before a race, because rested muscles typically produce faster times. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states a general rule: tapering usually produces faster times. Among Okafor's ultramarathoners, a long taper produced slower times. The specific case breaks the rule, so you need a contrast word, 'by contrast.'

A.why: This is the classic trap. A specific group of runners follows a general claim, so it looks like an example. But those runners got slower after tapering, which contradicts the claim that tapering produces faster times. An example has to agree with what it illustrates.

C.why: 'Thus' says the second sentence follows from the first. Slower times after tapering do not follow from a rule that tapering speeds athletes up. They cut against it.

D.why: 'Furthermore' adds a point in the same direction. Try the 'and also' test: 'Tapering produces faster times, and also tapering produced slower times' sounds wrong because the second idea contradicts the first.

items.stimulus: Most dyers in medieval Europe guarded their recipes as trade secrets, passing formulas for fixing color to cloth only from master to apprentice and seldom committing them to paper. items.subtype_name: Two things set side by side (By contrast / Conversely)
items.stimulus: The Mercator projection preserves the angles between lines on a map, which made it invaluable to navigators plotting a constant compass heading, but it enlarges landmasses more and more the farther they lie from the equator. items.explanation: There are two subjects: the Mercator projection and equal-area projections. Mercator keeps shapes and angles but distorts size. Equal-area projections keep size but distort shape. The trade-off is reversed, so 'conversely' is the logical transition.

C.why: 'In addition' adds another point in the same direction. Here the second projection keeps exactly what the first one distorts and distorts what the first one keeps. That is an opposition, not an addition.

D.why: 'Hence' presents the second sentence as a result of the first. The Mercator projection's features do not produce the Gall-Peters projection's features. The passage sets two separate designs side by side.

items.subtype_name: Parallel lines / intersecting lines: one angle relationship
items.stimulus: An ornithologist sketches a hawk's straight glide path, line $t$, as it crosses two parallel power lines, $m$ and $n$. In the figure, line $t$ intersects line $m$ and then line $n$. Where $t$ meets $m$, the angle above $m$ and to the right of $t$ is labeled $116^\circ$. Where $t$ meets $n$, the angle above $n$ and to the right of $t$ is labeled $x^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: In the figure, line $m$ is parallel to line $n$. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Both angles sit above their parallel line and to the right of the transversal, so they are corresponding angles. Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel, so $x = 116$.

A.why: You subtracted 90 from 116, as if the angles were complementary. Nothing in the figure makes a right angle.

B.why: You treated the angles as supplementary and found $180 - 116$. Angles in matching positions are equal, not supplementary.

D.why: You used the 360-degree rule for angles around a point. These two angles are at different intersections, and the rule doesn't apply to them.

items.subtype_name: Present a study's aim, method, or conclusion
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Self-healing concrete contains bacterial spores that produce limestone when water seeps into cracks.
• Engineers led by Priya Raman wanted to know whether such concrete could repair itself in cold climates.
• They cast 60 test beams, cracked them, and stored them at 4°C for 90 days.
• Cracks narrower than 0.4 mm sealed completely; wider cracks sealed only partly.
• The team concluded that the concrete is suitable for cold-climate use only where cracks are expected to stay small.
items.stem: The student wants to present the conclusion that Raman's team reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: In Raman's study, cracks narrower than 0.4 mm sealed completely at 4°C, while wider cracks sealed only partly.
Raman's team concluded that self-healing concrete can fully seal cracks of any width, even in cold climates.
Raman's team wanted to know whether concrete containing bacterial spores could repair itself in cold climates.
Raman's team concluded that self-healing concrete suits cold climates only where cracks are expected to stay small.
items.explanation: A conclusion is the interpretation the researchers drew from their results, and the last note gives it. Choice D restates it: the concrete is suitable for cold climates only where cracks will stay small.

A.why: This is the finding, the raw result about crack widths. The conclusion is what the team decided those results mean for real-world use, and that isn't stated here.

B.why: It uses the word 'concluded,' but it reverses the notes. Wider cracks sealed only partly, so the team did not conclude that cracks of any width would seal.

items.subtype_name: Pythagorean theorem: find the missing side
items.stimulus: An earthquake's hypocenter is $F$, which lies directly below its epicenter $E$ on the ground. Seismic station A is on level ground $20$ kilometers from $E$, and the straight-line distance from station A to $F$ is $29$ kilometers. Seismic station B is also on level ground, $72$ kilometers from $E$. Treat the ground as a flat plane.
items.stem: What is the distance, in kilometers, between station B and the hypocenter?
items.explanation: Segment $EF$ is vertical, so it makes a right angle with the ground. In the triangle with station A, the $29$ km distance to $F$ is the hypotenuse, so you subtract to find the depth: $EF = \sqrt{29^2 - 20^2} = \sqrt{841 - 400} = \sqrt{441} = 21$ km. For station B, the two legs are $72$ and $21$, so the distance is $\sqrt{72^2 + 21^2} = \sqrt{5184 + 441} = \sqrt{5625} = 75$ km.

A.why: $21$ km is the depth of the hypocenter. You found that from station A and stopped there, before using it as a leg in station B's triangle.

C.why: You used $29$ as the depth. But $29$ km is the slanted distance from station A to the hypocenter, not $EF$, so you got $\sqrt{72^2 + 29^2}$.

D.why: In station A's triangle you added the squares, $29^2 + 20^2 = 1241$, when you should have subtracted. The $29$ km distance is the hypotenuse, so the depth is a leg. That wrong depth squared then carried into $\sqrt{5184 + 1241}$.

items.explanation: The east and north legs meet at a right angle, so the straight-line distance of $4\sqrt{5}$ km is the hypotenuse. First, $(4\sqrt{5})^2 = 16 \cdot 5 = 80$. The north leg is $\sqrt{80 - 8^2} = \sqrt{80 - 64} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ km.

items.stimulus: A paleobotanist is cataloguing a rectangular slab of shale that holds a fossilized fern frond. The slab is $3\sqrt{2}$ decimeters wide. The frond lies along a diagonal of the slab, which runs from one corner to the opposite corner and is $3\sqrt{6}$ decimeters long.
items.stem: What is the length, in decimeters, of the slab?
items.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse. Square each given side: $(3\sqrt{6})^2 = 9 \cdot 6 = 54$ and $(3\sqrt{2})^2 = 9 \cdot 2 = 18$. The length is $\sqrt{54 - 18} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ decimeters.

A.why: You squared only the radicals and not the coefficient $3$, so you got $18$ and $6$ instead of $54$ and $18$. That gave $\sqrt{18 - 6} = \sqrt{12}$.

B.why: You added $54 + 18 = 72$, which treats the diagonal as a leg. The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse, so the missing side comes from subtracting.

D.why: $36$ is the square of the length. You found $54 - 18 = 36$ but didn't take the square root.

items.subtype_name: Pythagorean theorem: find the missing side
items.stimulus: A folklorist is retracing a village legend on flat ground. According to the legend, a traveler starts at a standing stone, walks $24$ paces due north, and then walks due east until reaching a well that is exactly $40$ paces from the stone in a straight line. From the well, the traveler walks $36$ paces due north to an old hawthorn tree.
items.stem: What is the straight-line distance, in paces, between the standing stone and the hawthorn?
items.explanation: In the first triangle, the $40$ paces from stone to well is the hypotenuse, so the eastward leg is $\sqrt{40^2 - 24^2} = \sqrt{1600 - 576} = \sqrt{1024} = 32$ paces. D.why: $60$ paces is only the total northward distance. The hawthorn is also $32$ paces east of the stone, so the straight-line distance has to include that leg.

items.stimulus: A meteorologist launches a weather balloon attached to the ground by a taut, straight $260$-meter cable. At first, the balloon is directly above a point on level ground $100$ meters from the cable's anchor. items.subtype_name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
items.stimulus: A sports scientist filming a volleyball serve modeled the ball's height above the floor with the function $h(t) = -5t^2 + 13t + 1.5$, where $h(t)$ is the height, in meters, $t$ seconds after the serve. The model shows the ball at a height of 5.9 meters when $t = 0.4$.
items.stem: At what other time $t$, in seconds, is the ball's height 5.9 meters?
items.explanation: The vertex is at $t = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{13}{2(-5)} = 1.3$. A parabola is symmetric about its vertex, so a height reached 0.9 seconds before the peak is reached again 0.9 seconds after it: $2(1.3) - 0.4 = 2.2$. Check: $h(2.2) = -24.2 + 28.6 + 1.5 = 5.9$.

A.why: 1.3 seconds is when the ball reaches its highest point, which is the vertex. You found the axis of symmetry but didn't use it to find the matching time on the far side of the peak.

B.why: You added 0.4 to the vertex time. The matching time is the same distance past the vertex as 0.4 is before it, so you need $1.3 + (1.3 - 0.4)$, not $1.3 + 0.4$.

D.why: You doubled the vertex time and forgot to subtract 0.4. 2.6 seconds is actually when the ball comes back down to its starting height of 1.5 meters, not to 5.9 meters.

items.subtype_name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
items.stimulus: A musicologist studying recordings of a symphony models how the conductor's tempo drifts from the marked tempo. The function $d(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, gives the deviation from the marked tempo, in beats per minute, $x$ minutes into the movement. In the xy-plane, the graph of $y = d(x)$ has its vertex at $(4, -6)$ and crosses the x-axis at two points.
items.stem: Which of the following could be the value of $c$?
items.explanation: In vertex form, $d(x) = a(x - 4)^2 - 6$. The vertex is below the x-axis, so the graph can only cross the axis twice if it opens upward, which means $a > 0$. Expanding gives $c = 16a - 6$, and with $a > 0$ that means $c > -6$. Only 10 works, with $a = 1$: $(x - 4)^2 - 6$ has two real roots.

A.why: This value comes from $a = -1$. A parabola that opens downward from a vertex at $y = -6$ never reaches the x-axis, so it can't have two x-intercepts.

B.why: You used a vertex of $(4, 6)$. With that vertex, a downward-opening parabola would cross twice, and $a = -\frac{1}{4}$ gives $c = -10$. With the actual vertex $(4, -6)$, though, $a = -\frac{1}{4}$ opens downward and never crosses the axis.

C.why: $-6$ is the y-coordinate of the vertex, not the y-intercept. $c = -6$ would also need $a = 0$, and then the function wouldn't be quadratic at all.

items.subtype_name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
items.stimulus: An astronomer tracking a comet from an observatory modeled its altitude above the horizon with the function $A(t) = -2t^2 + 14t - 12$, where $A(t)$ is the altitude, in degrees, $t$ hours after 8:00 p.m., for $1 \le t \le 6$.
items.stem: According to the model, how many hours after 8:00 p.m. does the comet reach its greatest altitude?
items.explanation: The greatest altitude is at the vertex, where $t = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{14}{2(-2)} = 3.5$. You can confirm this with the roots: $A(t) = -2(t - 1)(t - 6)$, and 3.5 is halfway between 1 and 6.

B.why: 6 is a root of the model, the time when the comet sinks back to the horizon at 0 degrees. It isn't the time of greatest altitude.

C.why: You divided 14 by 2 and left out the leading coefficient. The denominator is $2a = 2(-2) = -4$, not 2.

D.why: 12.5 degrees is the greatest altitude itself, the y-coordinate of the vertex. The question asks when it happens, which is the x-coordinate.

items.stimulus: A civil engineer designing a concrete footbridge arch models its shape with the function $h(x) = -0.05x^2 + bx$, where $b$ is a constant and $h(x)$ is the height of the arch, in meters, above the road at a horizontal distance of $x$ meters from one base. The arch reaches its maximum height at $x = 30$.
items.stem: What is the maximum height, in meters, of the arch above the road?
items.explanation: The vertex is at $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$, so $30 = -\frac{b}{2(-0.05)} = 10b$, which gives $b = 3$. Then $h(30) = -0.05(900) + 3(30) = -45 + 90 = 45$ meters.

A.why: 3 is the value of $b$, which you need along the way. You still have to substitute $x = 30$ back into $h(x)$ to get the height.

C.why: 60 is the other root, where the arch meets the road again. It's the span of the arch, not its height.

D.why: You evaluated only the $bx$ term and dropped $-0.05(30)^2 = -45$.

items.stimulus: A labor economist studying a backward-bending labor supply curve models the average number of hours worked per week with the function $f(w) = -0.02w^2 + bw + 20$, where $b$ is a constant and $f(w)$ is the number of hours when the hourly wage is $w$ dollars. The model predicts the same number of weekly hours at a wage of 15 dollars as at a wage of 35 dollars.
items.stem: According to the model, what is the maximum number of hours per week the workers supply?
items.explanation: Because $f(15) = f(35)$, the vertex is halfway between them, at $w = 25$. Then $25 = -\frac{b}{2(-0.02)} = 25b$, so $b = 1$. The maximum is $f(25) = -0.02(625) + 25 + 20 = -12.5 + 45 = 32.5$ hours.

D.why: You treated $-0.02(625)$ as $+12.5$. The squared term is negative because the leading coefficient is negative, so it subtracts from the total.

items.subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim
items.stimulus: Slow slip events are episodes in which a section of fault creeps for days or weeks without producing noticeable shaking. They have often been described as a safety valve that bleeds off stress that might otherwise be released in a damaging earthquake. After analyzing a decade of GPS records from the Tavora subduction zone, seismologist Lucía Ortega contends that the valve metaphor is misleading, because slow slip can shift stress onto neighboring sections of the fault that remain locked.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by a seismologist would best support Ortega's claim?
choices: "Slow slip episodes at Tavora recurred roughly every fourteen months, a regularity that let researchers place instruments along the fault before each one began."
"After each slow slip episode, small earthquakes grew more frequent along the adjacent locked section, and borehole instruments there recorded a clear rise in strain."
"Within the creeping section itself, strain dropped sharply after each slow slip episode, falling to levels lower than any measured between episodes."
"Strain on the locked sections next to the creeping zone stayed essentially unchanged during each slow slip episode and in the months that followed."
items.explanation: Ortega's claim is specifically about where the stress goes: slow slip moves stress onto neighboring locked sections. Choice B reports rising strain and more small earthquakes in exactly that place, the adjacent locked section, right after each episode. That is the transfer the claim describes.

A.why: You picked a true-sounding detail about slow slip, its regular timing, that says nothing about stress moving to other parts of the fault.

C.why: This is the trap. The quotation is about the right subject, but it shows stress being released on the section that slipped, which is the 'safety valve' view. It says nothing about the neighboring locked sections the claim is about.

D.why: Unchanged strain on the adjacent locked sections would count against Ortega's claim. You matched the location the claim names but missed that the direction is reversed.

items.stimulus: Meteor showers occur when Earth passes through trails of debris shed by comets. Because fresh trails are denser, astronomers have generally expected the most intense showers to come from debris released most recently. After reviewing records of forty meteor outbursts, astronomer Kwame Asante concludes that a trail's age matters less than whether Jupiter's gravity has compressed it into a narrow band that Earth then crosses.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by an astronomer would best support Asante's conclusion?
choices: "Trails released within the last few decades were consistently denser than older trails, holding several times as many particles in each cubic kilometer."
"Jupiter's gravity can also nudge whole debris trails out of Earth's path, which explains why several confidently predicted showers never appeared."
"The most intense outbursts in the historical record all came from debris that the parent comets had shed within the preceding fifty years."
"Several of the strongest outbursts came from centuries-old trails that Jupiter had squeezed into tight ribbons, while younger, uncompressed trails produced modest displays."
items.explanation: Asante's conclusion has two parts: age matters less, and compression by Jupiter matters more. Choice D shows both. Old but compressed trails produced strong outbursts, while younger trails that weren't compressed produced weak ones.

A.why: This is the trap. It is about debris trails and their age, but it only shows that young trails are denser. That was the old premise. It says nothing about which trails produce the most intense showers or about compression by Jupiter.

B.why: You matched the mention of Jupiter's gravity, but this describes a different effect, moving trails out of Earth's path. It doesn't show that compressed trails give stronger showers.

C.why: If the strongest outbursts all came from recent debris, trail age would matter most. That is the view Asante rejects.

items.stimulus: Versions of the tale of the clever miller, who outwits a greedy landlord by hiding grain in a dry well, have been recorded from the Baltic coast to the shores of the Caspian Sea. Some folklorists attribute the tale's wide range to independent invention, reasoning that grievances against landlords arose everywhere. Folklorist Irena Vasko disagrees, arguing that the tale traveled with merchants along river trade routes.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by a folklorist would best support Vasko's claim?

"In nearly every recorded version, the landlord's greed is punished in a way that mirrors his own offense, a pattern that listeners across the region clearly relished."
"Tales of peasants outwitting their landlords appear in collections from regions with no known contact with one another, from rural Portugal to Korea."
"The earliest written version of the tale, preserved in a monastery chronicle, dates to the fourteenth century, although its oral origins are probably older."

C.why: Similar tales in regions with no contact are evidence for independent invention, the position Vasko argues against.

items.stimulus: In many mountain watersheds, beavers build dams that slow streams and spread water across floodplains. "During the dry summer of 2021, reaches below beaver complexes kept flowing into September, while comparable reaches without dams went dry by late July."
"Beaver populations in the region have rebounded since trapping limits were introduced, and active dams are now found on most of its tributaries."

items.subtype_name: Which quotation from a scholar, survey or article supports the claim
items.stimulus: Farmers who plant cereal rye in autumn and cut it down before sowing soybeans often find fewer weeds in their fields. Rye residue releases compounds that can suppress seed germination, and it also forms a mat that blocks light from reaching the soil surface. Agronomist Priya Nandakumar claims that the mat's shading, rather than its chemistry, accounts for most of this weed suppression.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by an agronomist would best support Nandakumar's claim?
choices: "Plots covered with rye residue had roughly 70 percent fewer weeds than bare plots, and the difference between the two held steady through midsummer."
"In plots where rye residue was rinsed repeatedly to strip out its suppressive compounds, weeds stayed nearly as sparse as under untreated residue."
"When rye residue was ground into powder and mixed into bare soil, weed germination fell almost as much as it did beneath an intact mat."
"Soybean yields in rye-covered plots matched those in plots treated with herbicide, which makes the cover crop an economical choice for many farms."
items.explanation: The claim compares two possible causes. It says shading does most of the work, not chemistry. Choice B removes the chemistry and keeps the mat, and suppression barely changes. That isolates shading as the main cause.

A.why: This is the trap. It confirms that rye residue suppresses weeds, but the claim is about which cause is responsible. This comparison with bare plots can't tell shading apart from chemistry.

C.why: Powdered residue gives no shade, so strong suppression here would point to chemistry. That goes against Nandakumar's claim.
